cards.title: Iran War Exposes Limits of U.S. Power and Accelerates Perceptions of Imperial Decline
cards.background: In an Al Jazeera interview published on 2026-05-11, economist Richard Wolff argues that the United States is facing a long decline in global power and that the Iran war has trapped Washington in a position where it is 'not in control but can't walk away.' He claims U.S. threats to 'take over countries and destroy civilisations' reflect a weakening empire rather than strength, and says people around the world are internalising the lesson that the U.S. cannot easily defeat Iran. Wolff also points to domestic inequality, saying the richest 10 percent of Americans own 80 percent of corporate stocks, making the stock market irrelevant to most Americans.

prop_args.thesis: The Iran war accelerates U.S. imperial decline by exposing the gap between American military reach and its inability to impose political outcomes.
mechanisms: First, the war reveals strategic overextension. This is because (1) the U.S. can project force into the Middle East, but (2) it cannot convert that force into decisive victory or stable control, and (3) repeated stalemates teach allies and rivals that American threats are less credible than before.

Second, the conflict damages U.S. deterrence by normalizing the idea that Washington is trapped. Three reasons: one, if the U.S. is 'not in control but can't walk away,' adversaries learn escalation can be managed without capitulation; two, partners hedge rather than fully align with Washington; three, the aura of omnipotence that underpins empire erodes when even a major regional war does not produce clear dominance.

Third, the domestic political economy makes decline harder to reverse. This matters because (1) wealth is concentrated among the top 10 percent who own 80 percent of corporate stocks, so most Americans do not materially benefit from financial-market strength; (2) public anger rises when foreign policy costs are socialized while gains are captured by elites; and (3) declining domestic legitimacy reduces the state’s ability to sustain long, expensive imperial commitments.

opp_args.thesis: The U.S. is not in terminal decline; it remains the only power with the global military, financial, and alliance capacity to shape outcomes even in a difficult war.
mechanisms: First, military difficulty is not the same as imperial collapse. One, great powers often fail to achieve clean victories in asymmetric conflicts without losing systemic primacy; two, the U.S. still retains unmatched force projection, intelligence, logistics, and basing networks; three, being 'stuck' in a conflict can still mean the U.S. is the indispensable actor that all sides must respond to.

Second, the global order still runs through U.S.-centered institutions and markets. One, allies continue to depend on U.S. security guarantees; two, the dollar and American capital markets remain central to global finance; three, even critics of U.S. policy are reacting to U.S. power rather than replacing it with an alternative hegemon.

Third, internal inequality does not automatically translate into geopolitical decline. One, elite concentration can coexist with high state capacity and sustained military spending; two, stock ownership concentration does not negate the broader economic and technological base of the U.S.; three, domestic polarization often produces retrenchment or selective engagement, not the end of empire.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether visible strategic frustration equals structural decline. Prop wins if it proves that repeated inability to impose outcomes destroys deterrence, alliance confidence, and domestic legitimacy; opp wins if it shows the U.S. still retains the core institutions and coercive capacity that define hegemonic power.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would disengage from Middle Eastern wars
THBT the era of American unipolarity is over
THP a world where U.S. military dominance no longer guarantees political outcomes
data_points: Richard Wolff says the richest 10 percent of Americans own 80 percent of corporate stocks
Wolff describes the U.S. as 'not in control but can't walk away' from the Iran war
The article frames the conflict as evidence that the U.S. cannot 'defeat Iran' decisively

cards.title: European Refusal to Escort Hormuz Shipping Risks Normalizing Iranian Maritime Coercion
cards.region: Iran / Strait of Hormuz / United States / Europe
cards.background: The article argues that after a U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran, the United States began escorting commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz and asked European allies to contribute frigates. The piece says the U.S. blockade/escort effort began on April 13, six weeks into the war, and that American ships have already guided two commercial vessels and sent two destroyers through the strait despite Iranian attacks. It also notes that Saudi Arabia reportedly temporarily cut off access to American air bases after receiving no advance warning about the operation.

prop_args.thesis: European states should send frigates to the Strait of Hormuz because freedom of navigation is a core international norm that matters more than their anger at Trump.
mechanisms: First, escorting ships prevents Iran from turning a temporary wartime disruption into a permanent toll-taking regime. This is because (1) if Tehran can extract fees or impose de facto passage conditions once, it establishes a precedent that international waterways can be coerced, (2) other revisionist states learn that maritime chokepoints are bargaining chips, and (3) the credibility of the rules-based order depends on physically enforcing access, not merely condemning violations.

Second, Europe has a direct material interest in keeping Hormuz open even if the United States can partially absorb the shock. Three reasons: one, Europe is more import-dependent on Gulf energy flows than the U.S.; two, oil markets are global, so even U.S. exporters still face price spikes and inflation spillovers; three, European shipping and insurance sectors are exposed to higher risk premiums if convoy protection is absent.

Third, participating now is strategically smarter than waiting for a clean postwar moment. This matters because (1) the conflict is already ongoing and may recur in multiple rounds, (2) naval power is meant to operate in contested environments rather than only after victory, and (3) visible allied burden-sharing reduces the chance that Trump interprets European nonparticipation as free-riding and retaliates against NATO or U.S.-Europe security ties.

prop_args.thesis: Sending frigates is the least bad way for Europe to constrain Iranian coercion while preserving its own long-term security interests.
mechanisms: First, a multinational escort force raises the cost of Iranian harassment without requiring a full-scale war. This works because (1) frigates are designed for convoy protection and can deter small-boat, missile, or harassment attacks, (2) a coalition presence complicates Iran's targeting calculus by increasing the risk of escalation against multiple states, and (3) limited naval deployment is a proportionate response compared with broader military escalation.

Second, Europe cannot rely on diplomacy alone to stop Iran's regional behavior. Three reasons: one, the article argues that negotiations, sanctions, and limited strikes have not halted Iran's nuclear and regional ambitions; two, Iran's longer-range missiles can already threaten European capitals, so this is not a distant Gulf problem; three, if Europe refuses to act now, it signals that coercion works and invites more pressure later.

Third, allied participation preserves leverage over the United States rather than surrendering it. This matters because (1) if Europe helps, it can demand consultation and restraint in future operations, (2) if it refuses, Trump is more likely to punish Europe by weakening NATO commitments or withdrawing forces, and (3) cooperation on a narrow shared interest is a way to separate tactical disagreement from strategic alliance collapse.

opp_args.thesis: Europe should refuse to send frigates because doing so rewards reckless U.S. unilateralism and drags allies into a conflict they did not choose.
mechanisms: First, participation creates moral hazard for Washington. This happens because (1) if the U.S. can launch strikes without consultation and still receive allied military support, it learns that alliance costs are externalized, (2) Trump faces less domestic and diplomatic pressure to coordinate in future crises, and (3) allies lose the ability to condition cooperation on minimum standards of consultation.

Second, a naval deployment exposes Europe to escalation risk without giving it control over strategy. Three reasons: one, Iranian retaliation could target European ships, bases, or energy infrastructure; two, once frigates are present, any incident can spiral into a wider conflict that Europe did not authorize; three, Europe becomes a co-belligerent in a war whose objectives and end state are defined by Washington and Tel Aviv.

Third, refusing support is a necessary signal that alliance behavior has consequences. This matters because (1) Trump has already insulted allies and threatened Greenland, (2) if Europe always shows up regardless of U.S. behavior, deterrence against future abandonment or humiliation disappears, and (3) short-term shipping disruption may be preferable to normalizing a world where the U.S. can demand military help after blindsiding allies.

opp_args.thesis: The better response is to de-escalate and diversify energy and shipping security, not militarize Hormuz.
mechanisms: First, naval escorts do not solve the underlying conflict and may prolong it. This is because (1) Iran's incentives to resist are driven by regime security and regional rivalry, not just shipping access, (2) a visible foreign flotilla can be framed domestically in Iran as aggression, strengthening hardliners, and (3) military presence may harden the conflict into a long-term standoff rather than reopening diplomacy.

Second, Europe has alternative tools that reduce dependence on Hormuz over time. Three reasons: one, it can accelerate energy diversification and strategic reserves; two, it can use sanctions, insurance regulation, and diplomacy to reduce exposure; three, investing in resilience is less escalatory than sending warships into a live conflict zone.

Third, the article overstates the necessity of immediate military action. This matters because (1) the U.S. has already managed to escort some vessels successfully, (2) if the passage is partially secured, Europe can wait and assess rather than rush in, and (3) prudence is especially justified when the initiating actor was the Trump administration acting without allied consent.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether immediate enforcement of freedom of navigation outweighs the alliance-cost of rewarding Trump’s unilateralism. Pro-frigate arguments have the structural advantage on material security and precedent-setting, while opposition is strongest on alliance discipline and escalation risk; the round likely turns on whether debaters prioritize long-term maritime norms or short-term deterrence of U.S. recklessness.
motion_areas: TH, as Europe, would send frigates to escort shipping through the Strait of Hormuz
THBT European states should cooperate with U.S.-led maritime security operations even after unilateral American strikes
THP a world where allies condition military support on prior consultation before joint operations
THBT states should prioritize freedom of navigation over punishing allies for strategic disrespect

The U.S. has already guided two American commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz
The U.S. has also sent two destroyers through the strait

cards.title: Continued Fighting in Lebanon Risks Escalating Into a Wider Regional Security Breakdown
cards.background: Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands reported on 11 May 2026 that Lebanon is experiencing “days of deadly attacks” amid continued fighting. The article is a short video update and does not provide detailed casualty figures, named belligerents, or a ceasefire framework in the text provided. The key factual takeaway is that violence in Lebanon remains active and ongoing as of 11 May 2026.

prop_args.thesis: Ongoing violence in Lebanon will intensify regional instability by raising the costs of containment and increasing the chance of spillover.
mechanisms: First, continued fighting normalizes cross-border escalation. This is because (1) armed actors learn that limited attacks can be sustained without immediate decisive punishment, (2) each retaliatory cycle expands the set of acceptable targets and response thresholds, and (3) neighboring states and non-state actors are pulled into a tit-for-tat logic that is hard to stop once established.

Second, the conflict weakens Lebanon’s already fragile state capacity. Three reasons: one, repeated attacks divert security forces and political attention away from governance and border control; two, economic and humanitarian strain reduce the state’s ability to police armed groups; three, institutional paralysis makes it harder to enforce any de-escalation agreement or monopoly on force.

Third, the humanitarian and displacement effects create secondary regional pressure. This matters because civilians fleeing violence increase burdens on local services, deepen sectarian and political tensions in host areas, and create incentives for external actors to intervene under the banner of protection or stabilization.

opp_args.thesis: The fighting may remain contained because Lebanon’s internal fragmentation and external deterrence make actors prefer limited, bounded escalation over all-out war.
mechanisms: First, major actors have incentives to avoid a full regional war. one, the costs of open escalation are extremely high for states and militias alike; two, external patrons often prefer leverage through pressure rather than total destruction; three, limited violence can be used to signal resolve without crossing red lines that would trigger broader intervention.

Second, Lebanon’s fragmented political landscape can actually cap escalation. one, no single actor may have the capacity to unify the battlefield or sustain a long campaign; two, competing domestic factions can create veto points against total mobilization; three, the need to preserve some internal legitimacy can restrain groups from actions that would devastate civilian infrastructure and public support.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the current violence is a temporary flare-up or the start of a self-reinforcing escalation cycle. Prop is strongest on structural spillover and state weakness, while Opp wins if they can show actors have strong incentives and capacity to keep violence bounded.
motion_areas: TH, as regional powers, would prioritize de-escalation in Lebanon over punitive retaliation
THBT external actors should condition aid to Lebanon on security-sector reform
THP a world where regional conflicts are managed through enforced containment rather than regime change
data_points: Article published on 11 May 2026
Text describes 'days of deadly attacks' and 'continued fighting in Lebanon'
No casualty figures, named factions, or ceasefire terms are provided in the supplied text

cards.title: Israeli Strikes on Active Rescue Operations Deepen the Lebanon War’s Escalation Spiral
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported that a Lebanese civil defence worker captured the moment an Israeli strike hit an active rescue operation in Toul, southern Lebanon. Emergency crews had entered a damaged building to search for survivors when the strike hit the site. The incident is part of the wider Israel-Lebanon conflict environment, where cross-border strikes have repeatedly targeted areas in southern Lebanon.

prop_args.thesis: Striking an active rescue operation is a strategic and legal escalation that hardens Lebanese resistance, increases civilian harm, and makes de-escalation politically harder for both sides.
mechanisms: First, it destroys the credibility of any claim that strikes are narrowly targeted. This is because (1) hitting emergency crews creates the perception of indiscriminate force, (2) it collapses trust in Israeli restraint among Lebanese civilians, and (3) it makes neutral humanitarian actors treat the battlespace as unsafe, reducing rescue capacity.

Second, it strengthens militant recruitment and local support for retaliation. Three reasons: one, civilian and first-responder casualties create immediate outrage and revenge incentives; two, armed groups can frame the strike as proof that Israel targets all Lebanese institutions, not just fighters; three, communities under repeated attack become more willing to tolerate escalation if they believe surrender does not protect them.

Third, it raises the diplomatic and operational cost of continued Israeli operations. This matters because every incident involving rescuers or medics increases pressure on allies, expands calls for investigations, and makes future strikes more likely to be interpreted through a war-crimes lens, which constrains freedom of action over time.

opp_args.thesis: The strike reflects the logic of a battlefield where militant entrenchment inside civilian areas forces militaries to act quickly, and the broader responsibility for civilian risk lies with the armed actors embedding themselves there.
mechanisms: First, if rescue teams are operating in an active strike zone, the military may be targeting a site it believes still contains fighters or military infrastructure. Numbered reasons: one, armed groups often use damaged buildings and dense urban terrain to conceal assets; two, delayed strikes can allow militants to relocate or booby-trap sites; three, rapid follow-up attacks can be intended to prevent regrouping rather than to target civilians.

Second, the incident can be used to justify stronger deterrence rather than restraint. Numbered reasons: one, if one side believes the other uses civilian spaces to shield operations, it has incentives to keep pressure high; two, signaling that rescue activity does not create immunity may reduce tactical exploitation of humanitarian windows; three, in asymmetric conflict, allowing militants to manipulate civilian protection norms can prolong war and increase total casualties.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the strike is treated as a one-off battlefield error or as evidence of a broader pattern of indiscriminate escalation. Prop wins if it can show repeated attacks on humanitarian actors systematically erode civilian protection and make the conflict more brutal; opp wins if it can frame the incident as a tragic but militarily rational consequence of fighting embedded armed groups.
motion_areas: TH, as Israel, would prioritize continued strikes on suspected militant infrastructure in southern Lebanon despite civilian risk
THBT states should not conduct military operations in areas where emergency responders are actively rescuing civilians
THP a world where humanitarian workers are granted protected ceasefire windows during active conflicts
data_points: The strike hit an active rescue operation in Toul, southern Lebanon
Emergency crews had entered a damaged building to search for survivors when it was struck
Published by Al Jazeera on 11 May 2026

cards.title: Middle East Shipping Diversions Raise Whale-Collision Risks Off South Africa
cards.region: South Africa / Middle East / Global shipping routes
cards.background: Scientists at the University of Pretoria’s Whale Unit warned that rerouted shipping around South Africa has increased the risk of ship strikes on whales off the country’s south-western coast. Since 2023, after Houthi rebels hijacked a British-owned vessel near Yemen, more cargo ships moving between Asia and Europe have avoided the Middle East and sailed around the Cape of Good Hope; IMF PortWatch data cited by AFP says 89 commercial vessels sailed around the Cape between March and April 2026, almost double the 44 in the same period in 2023. Professor Els Vermeulen told the BBC her team overlaid whale distribution models with shipping routes and found higher collision risk, but said the scale is hard to quantify because many strikes occur offshore and are not observed.

prop_args.thesis: Global shipping rerouting creates a negative externality that governments and firms must actively manage, because trade efficiency gains are being purchased through hidden ecological harm.
mechanisms: First, the rerouting concentrates vessel traffic along a narrower corridor near whale habitats. This is because (1) ships avoiding the Red Sea and Suez are now funneled around the Cape of Good Hope, (2) the article says traffic there nearly doubled from 44 vessels in March-April 2023 to 89 in the same period in 2026, and (3) more traffic in the same waters mechanically raises the probability of ship-whale collisions.

Second, the harm is systematically undercounted, which means markets and regulators will underreact. Three reasons: one, many strikes happen deep offshore; two, dead whales often sink rather than wash ashore, creating 'cryptic mortality'; three, without visible carcasses or reliable surveys, shipping firms do not internalize the true ecological cost of routing decisions.

Third, this is a classic case for operational mitigation rather than pure laissez-faire. This matters because (1) speed reductions and route tweaks can cut collision risk without fully disrupting trade, (2) the cost of these measures is relatively small compared with the value of the cargo being moved, and (3) if states ignore the issue, they normalize a race-to-the-bottom where the cheapest route wins and environmental damage is offloaded onto coastal ecosystems.

opp_args.thesis: The economic and security necessity of rerouting shipping outweighs the marginal ecological cost, especially when the alternative is exposure to conflict zones and major supply-chain disruption.
mechanisms: First, the rerouting is a rational response to real maritime insecurity. One, ships are avoiding the Middle East because of Houthi attacks and the broader US-Israel-Iran conflict environment; two, the primary duty of shipping firms is to protect crews, cargo, and vessels; three, forcing ships back through high-risk waters could increase insurance costs, delays, and the probability of catastrophic losses far beyond the whale-strike issue.

Second, the environmental harm is uncertain and likely manageable compared with the scale of global trade. One, the article explicitly says the number of whale strikes is hard to quantify; two, the evidence is based on modeled overlap rather than observed mass mortality; three, targeted measures like seasonal speed limits or route adjustments can reduce risk without imposing a blanket constraint on shipping.

Third, overregulating shipping routes can create broader economic spillovers. One, longer routes around Africa already raise freight times and costs for Asia-Europe trade; two, additional compliance burdens can worsen inflation and supply-chain volatility; three, if states start micromanaging every ecological externality on emergency routes, they may reduce the resilience of global commerce in wartime conditions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between visible, immediate trade/security costs and diffuse, undercounted ecological harm. Prop wins if it frames this as a preventable externality with cheap mitigation; opp wins if it convinces the room that the rerouting is a necessary wartime adaptation and that the whale damage is too uncertain to justify constraining commerce.
motion_areas: TH, as an international shipping regulator, would mandate speed limits on vessels rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope
THBT states should subsidize environmentally safer shipping routes even during geopolitical crises
THP a world where commercial shipping is forced to internalize ecological externalities from rerouting around conflict zones
data_points: 89 commercial vessels sailed around the Cape of Good Hope between March and April 2026, almost double the 44 in the same period in 2023
Rerouting around South Africa increased after a British-owned vessel was hijacked near Yemen in 2023
Scientists say many whale strikes occur offshore and are lost to 'cryptic mortality' because carcasses sink
Professor Els Vermeulen’s team presented findings to the International Whaling Commission

cards.title: Israel Moves to Create Special Military Tribunals and Death Penalty for Palestinians, Deepening Dual Legal Regimes
cards.background: A bill in Israel’s Knesset would create a special military tribunal in Jerusalem to try Palestinians detained over the October 7, 2023 attacks, with the power to impose the death penalty. The proposal, co-sponsored by Simcha Rothman and Yulia Malinovsky and backed by Justice Minister Yariv Levin, has rare support across coalition and opposition and has entered its final readings. It would allow courts to admit evidence obtained under coercive conditions, deviate from standard evidence and detention rules, and broadcast key trial moments publicly. Israel’s military courts already have a reported 99.74% conviction rate for Palestinians, while Israeli civilians accused of crimes against Palestinians are convicted at around 3% in civilian courts.

prop_args.thesis: Creating special tribunals and allowing capital punishment for October 7 detainees entrenches a discriminatory security state that destroys due process and radicalizes future conflict.
mechanisms: First, the bill normalizes mass conviction over individualized justice. This is because (1) it explicitly permits broad judicial discretion and deviations from standard evidence rules, (2) it allows evidence obtained under coercive conditions that may amount to torture, and (3) it is designed for mass prosecutions after large-scale arrests rather than case-by-case adjudication.

Second, it deepens Palestinian perceptions that the legal system is an instrument of domination rather than law. Three reasons: one, the court is built as a special military structure outside ordinary civilian safeguards; two, the public broadcasting of hearings turns proceedings into political theater; three, the asymmetry with Israeli civilians tried for violence against Palestinians reinforces the view of a two-tier system.

Third, it increases long-term insecurity by feeding grievance, recruitment, and retaliatory cycles. This matters because (1) death sentences and show trials create martyrs and propaganda for militant groups, (2) they undermine any future bargaining over prisoners and ceasefires, and (3) they make postwar reconciliation and reintegration far harder by associating the state with collective punishment.

opp_args.thesis: Israel is entitled to create exceptional procedures for October 7 suspects because the scale and gravity of the attacks justify stronger deterrence and wartime accountability.
mechanisms: First, the state has a compelling security rationale to incapacitate and deter perpetrators of mass atrocities. One, October 7 killed at least 1,139 people, mostly civilians; two, around 240 people were taken captive; three, ordinary criminal procedures may be too slow or weak for wartime terror cases.

Second, special tribunals can be defended as a response to evidentiary and logistical realities after mass attacks. One, large numbers of detainees require a dedicated court system to avoid backlog; two, military judges may have better access to battlefield intelligence and chain-of-command evidence; three, public proceedings can signal transparency and reassure a traumatized domestic audience.

Third, the policy may restore deterrence and political legitimacy after a catastrophic security failure. One, visible punishment can reassure Israeli society that the state can respond decisively; two, the threat of execution may deter future participation in mass attacks; three, bipartisan support suggests the measure reflects broad democratic demand rather than fringe extremism.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether exceptional wartime justice is a necessary security response or a permanent erosion of equal protection under law. Prop wins if the round prioritizes institutional legitimacy and long-term conflict reproduction; opp wins if the judge prioritizes deterrence, victim justice, and the state’s right to respond to mass atrocity.
motion_areas: TH, as Israel, would establish special tribunals for October 7 suspects
THBT states should permit exceptional wartime courts for mass atrocity suspects
THP a world where governments can use public show trials for terrorism cases
THBT the death penalty should be available for perpetrators of mass-casualty terror attacks
THBT democracies should prioritize deterrence over full due process in wartime terror prosecutions

cards.title: Chad’s Lake Chad Air Campaign Risks Killing Civilians and Deepening Boko Haram’s Control Over Local Economies
cards.region: Lake Chad region (Nigeria, Chad, Niger, Cameroon)
cards.background: Dozens of Nigerian fishermen are feared dead after Chad launched air strikes on Boko Haram in the Lake Chad basin, with a local fisheries leader estimating more than 40 deaths. Chad said its military carried out retaliatory 'intensive air strikes' after Boko Haram attacks on Chadian bases near Lake Chad last Monday and Wednesday, which reportedly killed at least 24 soldiers and two generals. The Lake Chad basin is a cross-border waterways-and-swamp region shared by Nigeria, Chad, Niger, and Cameroon, and has long been a stronghold for Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP).

prop_args.thesis: Chad’s air campaign is strategically self-defeating because it increases civilian harm, undermines local cooperation, and strengthens Boko Haram’s coercive control over the Lake Chad economy.
mechanisms: First, the strikes blur the line between militants and civilians in a densely mixed battlespace. This is because (1) fishermen and Boko Haram fighters are operating on the same islands, (2) air power cannot reliably distinguish boats and shoreline movement at speed, and (3) panic during strikes pushes civilians into overloaded boats and drowning risk, so even 'successful' attacks generate civilian deaths and anger.

Second, civilian casualties destroy the intelligence and logistics network that states need to fight insurgents in swamp terrain. Three reasons: one, local fishermen are the people who know the waterways, routes, and island hideouts; two, if they fear being targeted they stop cooperating, fleeing, or reporting militant movement; three, the state then loses the only low-cost human intelligence available in a region where access is already limited by deep water and Boko Haram-controlled canoes.

Third, the campaign entrenches Boko Haram’s shadow governance rather than weakening it. This matters because Boko Haram already controls access to fishing grounds, transports fishermen, and collects taxes from them; when the state bombs the area without protecting civilians, communities become even more dependent on militant-controlled transport and market access, which increases insurgent revenue and legitimacy.

opp_args.thesis: Chad’s strikes are a necessary counterinsurgency response because failing to hit Boko Haram’s island sanctuaries would leave the group free to keep killing soldiers and terrorizing the basin.
mechanisms: First, the state cannot allow Boko Haram to operate with impunity after attacks that reportedly killed at least 24 soldiers and two generals. One, if the military does not retaliate, Boko Haram learns that cross-border raids are low-cost; two, that encourages more attacks on bases and communities; three, it signals weakness to both militants and local populations, which can accelerate recruitment and defections.

Second, air power is one of the few tools available in the Lake Chad terrain. One, the basin is a huge network of waterways, swampland, and islands that makes ground pursuit slow and dangerous; two, Boko Haram can retreat to remote islands after attacks; three, without air strikes the military may be unable to reach those sanctuaries at all, so the alternative is de facto safe haven for insurgents.

Third, even imperfect strikes can disrupt militant mobility and revenue. One, forcing Boko Haram fighters to flee reduces their ability to tax fishermen and control transport; two, repeated pressure can make island bases less secure and more expensive to hold; three, over time this can weaken the group’s territorial grip even if some civilians are tragically caught in the fighting.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the military campaign meaningfully degrades Boko Haram faster than it alienates the civilian economy that sustains the basin. Prop wins if you prioritize long-run counterinsurgency: in a mixed civilian-militant environment, indiscriminate air power predictably hands Boko Haram more recruits, more fear, and more control. Opp wins if you prioritize immediate security: after deadly attacks on Chadian bases, the state may need to accept imperfect strikes to prevent insurgents from enjoying sanctuary and momentum.
motion_areas: TH, as Chad, would prioritize air strikes against Boko Haram even at the risk of civilian casualties
THBT states should not conduct counterterrorism air campaigns in areas where militants and civilians are intermingled
THP a world where counterinsurgency operations require strict civilian-protection thresholds before air strikes are authorized
TH, as Nigeria and Chad, would negotiate local access arrangements with fishermen rather than rely primarily on aerial force

cards.title: Lebanon’s Hezbollah Disarmament Fails Because the State Lacks Moral Legitimacy, Not Because of Pure Sectarian Loyalty
cards.background: In September 2025, the Lebanese government launched its most ambitious disarmament plan ever, including seizing weapons and deploying Lebanese Armed Forces south of the Litani River. The process stalled after U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, Hezbollah rocket fire into northern Israel, and Israel’s air and ground campaign in Lebanon, which the article says has killed more than 2,500 people and displaced over 1 million since March. A December 2025 survey by researchers at King’s College London surveyed more than 2,000 Lebanese citizens and conducted hourlong interviews with 300 participants to test why many Lebanese oppose disarming Hezbollah even when they do not politically support the group.

prop_args.thesis: Hezbollah cannot be sustainably disarmed unless the Lebanese state first rebuilds legitimacy, because public support for its weapons is driven more by state failure and grievance than by ideological loyalty.
mechanisms: First, disarmament collapses when citizens do not trust the state to monopolize force. This is because (1) fewer than 1 in 4 respondents said they trusted the government, (2) citizens who lost trust and felt injustice were 29 percentage points more likely to oppose disarmament, and (3) people will not surrender protection to an institution they see as corrupt, partial, and ineffective.

Second, the strongest driver is not sectarian identity or Hezbollah’s welfare network but grievance over unfair governance. Three reasons: one, sectarian ties raised political support for Hezbollah by 30 points but only raised opposition to disarmament by 3 points; two, poorer and more dependent respondents were slightly less likely to support Hezbollah, which undercuts the idea that services buy weapon legitimacy; three, even in Sunni/Maronite Akkar, where Hezbollah political loyalty is only 5 percent, 41 percent still oppose disarmament because the state is seen as absent.

Third, external coercion backfires because it reinforces the very grievance structure that sustains Hezbollah’s arms. This matters because (1) Israeli strikes have destroyed schools, hospitals, and municipal infrastructure, (2) that destruction gives the Lebanese state fewer tools to rebuild credibility, and (3) every failed coercive attempt makes Hezbollah’s claim that the state cannot protect citizens look more credible.

opp_args.thesis: Hezbollah can still be weakened and eventually disarmed through pressure, because security fears and institutional substitution can shift public opinion even if grievances remain.
mechanisms: First, the security environment creates real demand for Hezbollah’s weapons. One, more than half of respondents said they felt existentially threatened by Israel; two, one in five reported severe exposure to war and political violence since 2023; three, those with higher threat exposure were 17 percentage points more likely to want Hezbollah armed, so reducing the threat can reduce support for the militia.

Second, the state and its allies can gradually replace Hezbollah’s role by building capacity and cutting resources. One, the Lebanese army already made early gains seizing weapons and deploying south of the Litani; two, sanctions and conditional aid can constrain Hezbollah’s financing and logistics; three, if the state visibly improves service delivery and security, the public may shift from tolerating Hezbollah to accepting disarmament.

Third, the article itself shows political support for Hezbollah is low, which means the group is not invulnerable. One, only 18 percent express political support for Hezbollah; two, that suggests its armed status rests on contingent fear rather than deep mass enthusiasm; three, once the security balance changes, the gap between political loyalty and weapons support can narrow.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether Hezbollah’s weapons are sustained by immutable communal loyalty or by changeable perceptions of state legitimacy and security. The prop side wins because grievance is broader, cross-sectarian, and structurally tied to state collapse, meaning coercion alone cannot create consent; the opp side only wins if it can show that security threats are the primary driver and can be reduced faster than legitimacy can be rebuilt.
motion_areas: TH, as the Lebanese government, would prioritize rebuilding state legitimacy over coercive Hezbollah disarmament
THBT the United States should stop conditioning aid on immediate Hezbollah disarmament
THP a world where Hezbollah’s disarmament is negotiated only after comprehensive state reform
THBT external military pressure is counterproductive to disarming non-state armed groups
TH, as Lebanon, would seek a political settlement with Hezbollah before attempting forced disarmament

Israel’s campaign in Lebanon has killed more than 2,500 people and displaced over 1 million since March.

cards.title: E.On Takeover of Ovo Could Create UK Energy Giant and Test Consumer Protection in a Consolidating Market
cards.background: E.On has announced plans to buy UK energy supplier Ovo, in a deal that could be worth up to £600m, though the value has not been disclosed officially. E.On has 5.6 million customers and Ovo has four million, which would make the combined company Britain’s largest energy supplier, ahead of Octopus. The deal still needs regulatory approval later this year, and both firms say existing tariffs, service, and credit balances would be protected during the review and after any transfer.

prop_args.thesis: Allowing the takeover creates a larger, more stable supplier that can invest better and deliver a smoother energy transition.
mechanisms: First, scale improves financial resilience. This is because (1) a larger customer base spreads wholesale price shocks across more accounts, (2) the merged firm is less likely to fail in a volatile energy market, and (3) fewer supplier collapses reduce the need for costly government-backed customer rescues.

Second, consolidation can improve investment capacity. Three reasons: one, a bigger balance sheet makes it easier to fund electrification, flexibility, and grid-related services; two, the company can invest in digital systems and customer service at lower unit cost; three, it can better absorb the fixed costs of innovation in low-carbon products.

Third, the deal can support the transition to cleaner energy. This matters because a larger supplier can bundle heat pumps, smart tariffs, and demand-response products at scale, which helps normalize electrification and makes zero-carbon offerings commercially viable.

opp_args.thesis: The takeover should be blocked or tightly constrained because it reduces competition and gives a dominant supplier too much market power over households.
mechanisms: First, the merger increases concentration in a market where consumers already face switching frictions. One, energy is a necessity, so customers do not shop like they do for discretionary goods; two, many households stay on default or fixed tariffs and are slow to move; three, a larger incumbent can exploit this inertia through weaker future pricing discipline.

Second, consolidation can worsen service quality and innovation incentives. One, when firms face less competitive pressure, they have less reason to keep call centres, billing systems, and complaint handling high quality; two, fewer rivals means fewer experiments in tariff design and customer-facing green products; three, the promised efficiencies may be captured as profit rather than passed through as lower bills.

Third, the merger creates a precedent for further consolidation in a fragile sector. This matters because if regulators approve the creation of Britain’s largest supplier, other firms may pursue similar mergers, gradually entrenching an oligopoly that is harder to regulate and more likely to underdeliver for consumers.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether scale mainly lowers costs and improves resilience, or whether it mainly weakens competition in a market where consumers have limited bargaining power. Prop wins if it can show the merger prevents instability and funds transition investment; Opp wins if it argues that any efficiency gains are outweighed by long-run price and service harms in a necessity market.
motion_areas: TH, as the UK regulator, would block the E.On-Ovo merger
THBT governments should allow energy sector consolidation to fund the green transition
THP a world where household energy suppliers are capped at a maximum market share

cards.title: Japan Can Turn U.S. Middle East Demands Into Alliance Leverage Without Fully Subordinating Its Security Agenda
cards.background: The article compares the Trump-era confrontation with Iran to the George W. Bush administration’s post-9/11 wars, arguing that Japan’s response to the Iraq War offers lessons for today. During the War on Terror, Japan supported the U.S. through humanitarian missions in Afghanistan and logistical support in the Indian Ocean, while also trying to link Iraq policy to U.S. attention on North Korea. The piece notes that the 2002 Japan-U.S. Security Consultative Committee linked Iraq and North Korea in a joint statement, and that today Tokyo faces pressure over whether to dispatch the Maritime Self-Defense Force to secure shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

prop_args.thesis: Japan should use crises like the Iran conflict to extract concessions from the United States and expand its strategic autonomy, rather than simply acting as an obedient ally.
mechanisms: First, bargaining through alliance support converts Japan's loyalty into concrete security returns. This is because (1) the U.S. values Japanese participation in global security operations as proof of alliance credibility, (2) Tokyo can condition that support on U.S. attention to Japan's core threats like North Korea, and (3) the 2002 Iraq-North Korea linkage shows that even a junior ally can force issue bundling when its cooperation matters.

Second, selective burden-sharing lets Japan gain influence without overcommitting militarily. Three reasons: one, non-combat support such as logistics, intelligence, and maritime protection is easier for Japan to justify domestically than direct combat; two, these contributions still raise Japan's value to Washington; three, they allow Tokyo to shape the agenda while avoiding the full costs of expeditionary warfare.

Third, a more assertive alliance posture strengthens Japan's long-term diplomatic standing. This matters because (1) being seen as a passive client damages Japan's credibility with both the U.S. and other partners, (2) active participation in global security helps Japan build a wider network beyond the U.S., and (3) the article argues that the post-9/11 era expanded Japan's role on the international stage, which can be leveraged into broader deterrence and supply-chain diversification.

opp_args.thesis: Japan's attempts to leverage U.S. crises for bargaining power are limited and can trap Tokyo into supporting wars that do not serve its interests.
mechanisms: First, alliance dependence means Japan often cannot credibly refuse U.S. requests. One, the U.S. remains Japan's only formal ally and the backbone of its deterrence against North Korea and China; two, once Washington frames an issue as alliance-defining, Tokyo faces reputational costs for dissent; three, the article explicitly says the 2002 SCC meeting created conditions under which Japan 'could not decline' support for Iraq.

Second, issue-linkage can backfire by expanding Japan's obligations faster than its influence. One, supporting U.S. Middle East operations pulls Japan into geographically distant conflicts; two, the expected payoff on Japan's core concerns may never materialize, as shown by Iraq producing no WMDs and North Korea's capabilities growing anyway; three, the result is a security dilemma where Japan pays the costs of escalation without getting the strategic returns it sought.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether alliance bargaining actually produces usable leverage or just coerces Japan into costlier commitments. Prop wins if the round is about strategic autonomy and long-term alliance management; opp wins if the focus is on the structural asymmetry of the U.S.-Japan relationship, because Washington can impose agenda expansion far more easily than Tokyo can extract durable concessions.

THBT middle powers should leverage great-power crises to expand their strategic autonomy
THP a world where allies can bargain over support for overseas military operations
THBT Japan should refuse to be a passive security client of the United States

cards.title: Western Insurance and Sanctions Can Strangle China’s Oil Supply More Easily Than Naval Blockades
cards.region: China / Persian Gulf-Hormuz / Southeast Asia / Global shipping lanes
cards.background: In February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran, and Tehran responded by disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and gas trade. The article argues that the immediate choke point was not only military but financial: war-risk insurance premiums for tankers transiting Hormuz reportedly jumped from about 0.25% of hull value to 3%-10%, making many voyages uneconomic. It then extends the logic to China, noting that roughly 80% of China’s oil imports pass through the Strait of Malacca and that about 11 million of China’s 15-16 million barrels per day of oil consumption travel by sea through waters Beijing does not control.

prop_args.thesis: Western control over insurance, sanctions, and dollar finance gives the US a far more effective tool than naval blockade to coerce China’s energy security.
mechanisms: First, insurance markets can make shipping commercially impossible without firing a shot. This is because (1) war-risk premiums can jump from 0.25% to 3%-10% of hull value, (2) a $250 million tanker can see voyage insurance costs rise from $625,000 to $7.5 million, and (3) private insurers, banks, and shipowners will simply stop moving cargo once the economics break.

Second, the US can extend the choke point beyond the strait itself by using sanctions and designation risk. Three reasons: one, the Joint War Committee and Lloyd’s guidance shape global underwriting behavior; two, once a port, route, or terminal is listed as high-risk, premiums rise even if no shots are fired there; three, the threat follows the cargo to the destination, so Chinese ports like Ningbo, Shanghai, and Qingdao can be priced out even if tankers reroute around Malacca.

Third, this creates a scalable coercive lever against China in a Taiwan crisis. This matters because (1) China’s overland alternatives only cover about 1.5 million barrels per day versus roughly 7.9 million barrels per day moving through Malacca to China, (2) China’s domestic war-risk insurance capacity is too small to replace Lloyd’s-scale coverage, and (3) the shadow fleet can be targeted through inspectors, brokers, flag registries, and banks, making evasion costly and incomplete.

opp_args.thesis: China can partially insulate itself from maritime coercion through stockpiles, alternative routes, and a growing non-Western shipping-finance ecosystem.
mechanisms: First, China has buffers that reduce the immediate bite of any insurance shock. One, it holds a strategic stockpile of nearly 1.4 billion barrels of oil; two, it can draw on overland pipelines from Myanmar, Kazakhstan, and Russia; three, it can reroute some traffic through the Sunda or Lombok Straits to avoid Malacca-specific disruption.

Second, Beijing can build parallel institutions to blunt Western market power. One, the China P&I Club and a Hong Kong war-risk pool are designed to provide non-Lloyd’s coverage; two, state-backed insurers can be instructed to underwrite politically sensitive voyages; three, China can subsidize shipping and absorb losses in ways private insurers cannot.

Third, the shadow fleet and noncompliant actors make total interdiction unrealistic. This is because (1) China already moves an estimated 2.6 million barrels per day through shadow-fleet channels, about 22% of imports, (2) many tankers operate under flags of convenience and opaque ownership structures, and (3) sustained enforcement is costly, uneven, and vulnerable to evasion through ship-to-ship transfers and third-country intermediaries.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether financial chokepoints can substitute for physical blockade at scale. Pro-prop wins if you prioritize commercial feasibility and the fact that insurers, banks, and shipowners are highly risk-sensitive; opp wins if you believe China’s stockpiles, state capacity, and shadow fleet can absorb enough disruption to prevent coercion from becoming decisive.

THBT countries should prioritize financial chokepoints over military blockades in great power competition
THP a world where maritime insurance is internationally regulated to prevent geopolitical coercion
THBT China should decouple its energy security from global shipping finance
TH, as China, would build a state-backed shadow shipping and insurance system

cards.title: Muted Victory Day Attendance Shows Russia’s Growing Dependence on Central Asian Optics
cards.region: Russia / Kazakhstan / Uzbekistan / Kyrgyzstan / EU sanctions context
cards.background: On May 9, 2026, Russia held its 81st Victory Day parade in Red Square, shortened to 45 minutes and stripped of heavy equipment such as tanks and missile systems. Only five world leaders attended the parade, including Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Malaysia, and Laos, while the leaders of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan also met Vladimir Putin on May 8. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov had visited Moscow in late April after Kyrgyzstan was hit by EU secondary sanctions, and North Korean soldiers were also reported to have participated in the parade.

prop_args.thesis: Russia’s need for Central Asian leaders to show up publicly proves Moscow is becoming more diplomatically dependent on its neighbors, not the other way around.
mechanisms: First, the attendance itself becomes a scarce diplomatic asset. This is because (1) only five world leaders attended this year compared with 27 at the 80th anniversary in 2025, (2) Russia used Tokayev and Mirziyoyev’s presence as proof of 'true' and 'special' bilateral relations, and (3) when a great power has to publicly celebrate any visit as validation, that signals a loss of status and leverage.

Second, Central Asian leaders can extract concessions by offering symbolic recognition. Three reasons: one, Moscow needs visible partners to rebut isolation narratives after sanctions and the Ukraine war; two, leaders like Tokayev and Mirziyoyev can convert attendance into better treatment, state visits, or economic favors; three, the fact that Putin personally praised them shows Russia is paying reputational rent for their presence.

Third, this shifts the regional balance of power toward hedging rather than hierarchy. This matters because (1) Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan can diversify between Russia, China, and the West without fully breaking ties, (2) Russia cannot easily punish them without worsening its own isolation, and (3) the more Moscow needs 'friends' in public, the less credible its coercive dominance becomes.

opp_args.thesis: The parade shows that Central Asian states still need Russia enough to keep performing loyalty when it matters.
mechanisms: First, the relationship remains structurally asymmetric in Russia’s favor. one, Central Asian economies, labor markets, and security arrangements are still deeply tied to Russia; two, leaders continue to travel to Moscow for major symbolic events despite reputational costs; three, the fact that only Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan came this year suggests selective participation, not genuine autonomy.

Second, public attendance is a low-cost signal that preserves access to a much larger patron. one, these leaders can maintain working ties with Putin while avoiding open confrontation; two, they gain protection from retaliation, trade disruption, and migration pressure; three, the parade is a visible price to pay for continued access to Russian markets and security coordination.

Third, Russia’s reduced parade does not equal reduced power. one, the absence of heavy equipment was due to operational and security concerns, not diplomatic weakness; two, Putin still hosted foreign leaders and framed the event as a test of loyalty; three, the presence of North Korean soldiers shows Russia can still mobilize alternative partners despite sanctions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether symbolic attendance reflects Russian dependence or Central Asian dependence. Prop wins if the round is about long-term leverage and status, because Russia is the actor publicly seeking validation; Opp wins if the round is about hard material power, because Central Asia still has strong incentives to keep Moscow onside for trade, labor, and security.
motion_areas: TH, as Central Asian states, would publicly distance themselves from Russia
THBT secondary sanctions are an effective tool for weakening Russian influence in Central Asia
THP a world where middle powers can extract concessions by performing symbolic loyalty to great powers
THBT post-Soviet states should hedge between Russia and the West rather than align firmly with either

cards.title: Advanced Economies Misdiagnose Supply-Shock Inflation as a Monetary Problem
cards.region: United States / United Kingdom / advanced economies
cards.background: The article argues that inflation has risen again across advanced economies in 2025 and early 2026, but the drivers are geopolitical turmoil, higher energy prices, and fragile supply chains rather than excess demand. It notes that the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England have kept rates steady and described their stance as 'data dependent' amid slowing growth and renewed recession fears. The core claim is that interest-rate hikes are a poor tool for inflation driven by supply-side shocks.

prop_args.thesis: Central banks should not rely on interest-rate hikes to fight today’s inflation because the inflation is being caused by supply shocks, so tightening mainly destroys growth without fixing prices.
mechanisms: First, rate hikes do not address the source of the inflation. This is because (1) energy-price spikes are driven by geopolitics and commodity markets, not domestic borrowing costs, (2) supply-chain fragility raises costs through bottlenecks rather than overheating demand, and (3) higher rates cannot quickly increase shipping capacity, refinery output, or trade stability.

Second, tightening creates a recessionary trade-off that can be worse than the inflation itself. Three reasons: one, higher rates raise mortgage, business-loan, and credit-card costs, two, firms respond by cutting hiring and investment, and three, weaker growth can lock in unemployment and lower real incomes even if inflation only falls marginally.

Third, monetary overreaction can make inflation more persistent in the medium term. This matters because if central banks crush demand while supply remains constrained, they reduce productive capacity, discourage investment in energy and logistics, and leave economies more vulnerable to the next price shock.

opp_args.thesis: Even when inflation begins as a supply shock, interest-rate hikes are still necessary because they prevent second-round effects and anchor expectations.
mechanisms: First, inflation can become self-reinforcing if workers and firms expect it to continue. One, wage demands rise as households try to protect real incomes, two, firms pass higher labor costs into prices, and three, a temporary supply shock turns into broad-based inflation.

Second, central banks need credibility more than precision. One, if they appear unwilling to tighten, markets may assume they will tolerate higher inflation, two, long-term borrowing costs can rise as investors demand an inflation premium, and three, restoring credibility later may require even harsher tightening.

Third, rate hikes can still reduce demand in sectors where inflation is demand-sensitive. One, consumers cut discretionary spending, two, firms face weaker pricing power, and three, this can stop a supply shock from spreading across the whole economy.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether inflation is mostly a demand problem or a supply problem. The pro side wins if the judge believes the current shock is structurally outside central-bank control, because then rate hikes impose large recession costs for little inflation relief; the opposition wins if they persuade that expectations and credibility make tightening necessary even when the initial shock is external.
motion_areas: TH, as central banks, would not raise interest rates in response to supply-shock inflation
THBT advanced economies should prioritize growth over inflation targeting during external price shocks
THP a world where central banks cannot use interest rates to respond to inflation caused by energy and supply disruptions

The US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England have held interest rates steady while citing 'data dependence'

cards.title: UK Social Media Users Face a Two-Tier Internet as TikTok Monetises Privacy and Ad-Blocking
cards.background: TikTok will begin notifying UK users aged 18 and over that they can pay £3.99 per month for an ad-free version of the app, called TikTok Ad-Free. Users who do not subscribe will continue to see personalised ads, and TikTok says the change will roll out gradually over the next few months. The company says the move is part of a broader trend across platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and Snapchat, which have also introduced paid ad-free or reduced-ad subscriptions. TikTok says ads already help British businesses reach customers, while critics argue the model is part of a wider shift toward 'consent or pay' systems that monetise privacy.

prop_args.thesis: TikTok’s ad-free subscription is a legitimate consumer-choice model that lets platforms monetise privacy without eliminating free access.
mechanisms: First, it creates a clearer market price for privacy and attention. This is because (1) users who value an ad-free experience can pay directly instead of 'paying' with data, (2) the platform can segment users by willingness to pay rather than forcing one model on everyone, and (3) the existence of a free tier preserves access for users who cannot or will not pay.

Second, it improves platform sustainability and reduces dependence on intrusive ad targeting. Three reasons: one, subscription revenue diversifies income away from pure surveillance advertising; two, it gives firms an incentive to offer cleaner, less cluttered products; three, it can reduce pressure to maximise engagement through ever-more manipulative ad targeting and tracking.

Third, it can be pro-competition and pro-business for the wider ecosystem. This matters because (1) TikTok still shows sponsored creator content, so advertisers and creators retain a route to reach audiences, (2) British businesses still benefit from the free ad-supported tier, and (3) normalising paid privacy may push the market toward more transparent, user-controlled platform design.

opp_args.thesis: TikTok’s subscription entrenches a two-tier internet where privacy and a better user experience become luxuries for those who can afford them.
mechanisms: First, it converts a basic expectation of digital dignity into a paywall. One, users who refuse tracking are now forced to pay for what used to be an opt-out; two, the free tier becomes the degraded product with more intrusive profiling; three, this normalises the idea that privacy is a premium feature rather than a baseline right.

Second, it increases coercion and reduces meaningful consent. One, most users will not pay £3.99 every month, especially younger or lower-income users, so 'choice' is largely illusory; two, the platform can remove free opt-out settings and make tracking the default; three, the result is consent extracted under economic pressure rather than freely given.

Third, it strengthens the ad-tech model and harms democratic and consumer welfare. One, more personalised ads mean more data extraction and behavioural manipulation; two, platforms can use the subscription as cover to deepen profiling of the majority who stay on free tiers; three, this widens inequality in access to privacy, creating a structural advantage for wealthier users and a structural disadvantage for everyone else.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether 'choice' is real when the alternative is paying monthly to avoid tracking. Prop wins if the round is about consumer preference and sustainable platform funding; opp wins if the round is about privacy as a baseline right and the coercive effects of paywalled consent. The structural advantage sits with opp because the free tier remains the default for most users, so the policy’s practical effect is to normalise surveillance for the many and privacy for the few.

THBT platforms should be allowed to offer 'consent or pay' models for personalised advertising
THP a world where users can pay to opt out of data-driven advertising
THBT privacy online should be treated as a premium service rather than a default right

cards.title: Bosnia’s peacekeeper exit exposes the fragility of post-Dayton state supervision
cards.background: Christian Schmidt, the international high representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, has confirmed he is stepping down after serving since 2021. The office was created by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement and gives the high representative sweeping 'Bonn Powers' to impose decisions and remove officials who threaten the peace settlement. Schmidt repeatedly used those powers against Bosnian-Serb leader Milorad Dodik, who was later given a one-year prison sentence and a six-year ban from holding public office for defying the office's rulings. The BBC reports that Schmidt has lost support from the US, while Russia has long opposed his appointment and backs closure of the Office of the High Representative.

prop_args.thesis: Bosnia needs the Office of the High Representative to prevent ethno-nationalist leaders from dismantling the Dayton settlement.
mechanisms: First, the office is the only actor with credible coercive authority over Bosnia's fragmented political elites. This is because (1) domestic institutions are built around ethnic vetoes and power-sharing, (2) leaders like Milorad Dodik have repeatedly ignored ordinary legal and political constraints, and (3) the Bonn Powers allow the envoy to block separatist laws and remove obstructive officials.

Second, removing the office creates a security vacuum that separatists can exploit incrementally. Three reasons: one, Dodik has already tested the limits of the state by pushing separatist legislation; two, once the external enforcer disappears, each violation becomes a new baseline and normalizes defiance; three, Bosnia's fragile institutions lack the capacity to credibly punish escalation on their own.

Third, international supervision is still cheaper than a renewed crisis. This matters because (1) Bosnia's 1990s war was ruinous and the Dayton system exists precisely to prevent relapse, (2) a breakdown would likely require a far more expensive EU/NATO crisis response later, and (3) keeping a single supervisory office is a low-cost way to preserve deterrence and political stability.

opp_args.thesis: The Office of the High Representative has become an undemocratic foreign veto that entrenches Bosnia's dysfunction rather than solving it.
mechanisms: First, external supervision weakens domestic accountability. Numbered reasons: one, local politicians can blame the envoy for unpopular compromises instead of owning governance failures; two, voters never develop trust in domestic institutions if final authority always sits abroad; three, repeated intervention discourages coalition-building and normal parliamentary bargaining.

Second, the office creates a legitimacy crisis that fuels nationalist backlash. Numbered reasons: one, Schmidt's appointment was never approved by Russia and is now losing US support, so the office lacks unified great-power backing; two, leaders like Dodik can frame the envoy as an imposed colonial overseer, which mobilizes separatist sentiment; three, a contested foreign authority is easier to resist than a locally legitimate constitutional order.

Third, Bosnia needs a transition to self-government even if the process is messy. Numbered reasons: one, the post-Dayton model has lasted for decades, so indefinite tutelage is no longer a temporary fix; two, if the state cannot function without an external enforcer, that itself proves the current model is unsustainable; three, phasing out the office can force EU-style institutional reform and domestic responsibility.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether Bosnia's main risk is immediate separatist escalation or long-term institutional dependency. Prop wins if you think one credible external enforcer is the only thing stopping elite defection; Opp wins if you think the envoy has become a legitimacy sink that perpetuates the very ethnic politics it was meant to contain.
motion_areas: TH, as the international community, would maintain the Office of the High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina
THBT international peace agreements should include long-term foreign supervisory powers
THP a world where post-conflict states are supervised by external trustees until domestic institutions are fully functional
THBT Bosnia should prioritize domestic sovereignty over continued international oversight

cards.title: India-Vietnam Security Convergence Forces China to Confront a More Crowded Indo-Pacific
cards.region: China / India / Vietnam / South China Sea / Indian Ocean
cards.background: India and Vietnam established relations in 1972 and upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2016. On May 5-7, 2026, Vietnamese General Secretary To Lam visited India, and the two sides elevated ties again to an "Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership," with a joint declaration emphasizing defense industry cooperation and maritime support. The article says cooperation has moved beyond symbolic diplomacy into submarine training, fighter pilot training, maritime situational awareness, defense credit support, and possible BrahMos missile transfers, all of which China is watching closely because of their implications for the South China Sea and wider Indo-Pacific.

prop_args.thesis: India-Vietnam security cooperation is strategically significant because it creates a durable soft-balancing network that complicates China’s ability to dominate the Indo-Pacific without requiring a formal alliance.
mechanisms: First, it expands the number of capable actors China must deter at once. This is because (1) Vietnam sits on the western edge of the South China Sea, directly affecting China’s maritime perimeter, (2) India brings naval reach into the Indian Ocean and eastern maritime space, and (3) their coordination forces Beijing to plan for overlapping pressure points rather than a single front.

Second, it improves Vietnam’s denial capabilities in ways that raise the cost of Chinese coercion. Three reasons: one, submarine and fighter pilot training increases operational competence; two, maritime situational awareness makes it harder for China to operate below the threshold of open conflict; three, a potential BrahMos transfer would strengthen A2/AD and threaten Chinese naval freedom of action in contested waters.

Third, it normalizes middle-power security coordination outside formal alliances. This matters because (1) China cannot easily label or punish a treaty bloc, (2) incremental cooperation is harder to reverse than one-off diplomacy, and (3) the precedent encourages other regional states to hedge through similar networks, steadily eroding China’s preferred hierarchical order.

opp_args.thesis: India-Vietnam ties are still too limited to materially change the regional balance, so China’s concern is more symbolic than strategic.
mechanisms: First, both states retain strong constraints on escalation. One, Vietnam’s "four nos" policy prevents formal alignment against China; two, India’s strategic autonomy makes it unwilling to become a frontline anti-China proxy; three, without a binding alliance, cooperation remains reversible and politically shallow.

Second, the material scale of cooperation is still modest. One, the relationship has historically been driven by delegation exchanges and small-scale exercises; two, India’s defense-industrial base is not yet capable of supplying large-scale, high-end military transformation; three, economic and technological integration remain too weak to generate sustained strategic dependence.

Third, China can absorb this kind of hedging because it already faces stronger counterweights. One, the U.S.-Japan-Australia security architecture is far more consequential; two, India-Vietnam cooperation does not create a unified command structure or joint war plan; three, Beijing can respond bilaterally through trade, diplomacy, and coercive signaling without facing a consolidated bloc.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic balancing and structural balancing. Prop wins if the round is about long-term strategic environment, because even small cooperative steps can accumulate into a harder-to-control regional order; opp wins if the round is about immediate military balance, because the article itself concedes there is no alliance and no decisive shift in power.

THBT strategic autonomy is the most effective way for smaller states to hedge against great powers

cards.title: US-Iran Peace Talks Collapse Over Sequencing: Hormuz Reopening vs Nuclear Concessions
cards.region: Iran / United States / Gulf / Lebanon / Pakistan
cards.background: On Sunday, Iran sent a counterproposal to the US through mediator Pakistan after more than a month of faltering talks following a temporary ceasefire that began on April 8. Trump publicly rejected the response as “totally unacceptable,” while the two sides remain deadlocked over sequencing: the US wants Iran to first reopen the Strait of Hormuz and curb enrichment, while Iran wants an end to hostilities and the naval blockade before discussing its nuclear programme. The article says the Strait of Hormuz carries roughly one-fifth of global oil and natural gas exports in peacetime, and that Iran has about 440kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington wants transferred or diluted.

prop_args.thesis: Trump’s rejection is strategically rational because it prevents Iran from locking in sanctions relief and de-escalation without giving up the core capabilities that make its coercive leverage work.
mechanisms: First, the US cannot accept Iran’s sequencing because it would reward brinkmanship. This is because (1) Iran has used a de facto blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and regional disruption as bargaining leverage, (2) conceding first on sanctions or the blockade would signal that escalation pays, and (3) that creates a repeatable model for future Iranian coercion in any crisis.

Second, the US needs to preserve nonproliferation credibility. Three reasons: one, Iran is reportedly sitting on about 440kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent, which is already far beyond civilian needs; two, Tehran’s proposal only suspends enrichment for a shorter period and rejects dismantlement, meaning the breakout infrastructure remains intact; three, allowing a partial deal would normalize a threshold nuclear state and weaken the global norm against enrichment to weapons-adjacent levels.

Third, Trump’s hard line improves bargaining power by making the cost of noncompliance immediate. This matters because the US can still escalate economically and maritime pressure, and by refusing to concede early it keeps open the option of forcing Iran to choose between continued isolation and a more substantive deal.

prop_args.thesis: The US position is necessary to protect regional security because Iran’s proposal would freeze the current balance of power while leaving its proxies and maritime threats intact.
mechanisms: First, Iran’s plan separates the ceasefire from the hard security issues in a way that preserves its regional network. This is because (1) Tehran wants hostilities to end before nuclear talks, (2) it also wants Lebanon and proxy-related issues addressed on its terms, and (3) that would let Iran keep leverage through Hezbollah and other aligned groups while extracting concessions elsewhere.

Second, reopening Hormuz before a broader settlement would expose Gulf states and shipping to renewed coercion. Three reasons: one, the strait is a chokepoint for global energy flows, so any Iranian ability to threaten it is strategic leverage; two, the article notes continued ship interceptions and attacks even during talks, showing that partial de-escalation does not guarantee compliance; three, a premature reopening without verification would simply give Iran time to rearm and reconstitute pressure tools.

Third, Trump’s rejection signals to allies and adversaries that the US will not trade away deterrence for a fragile pause. This matters because Gulf partners, Israel, and European shippers all have incentives to see a durable settlement rather than a temporary lull that leaves the underlying security problem unresolved.

opp_args.thesis: Trump’s rejection is counterproductive because Iran’s proposal was the best available path to de-escalation and the US is demanding maximalist concessions it cannot realistically enforce.
mechanisms: First, the US is asking for too much upfront. One, it wants Iran to reduce enrichment to 0 percent and hand over or transfer its 440kg stockpile; two, it wants a long moratorium and broader regional concessions; three, Iran has no domestic incentive to accept terms that look like unilateral surrender, so the result is stalemate rather than compliance.

Second, sequencing matters because security first is the only politically sellable deal in Tehran. One, Iran is facing sanctions, asset freezes, and a naval blockade, so it needs visible relief before it can justify concessions; two, if the US refuses to lift pressure first, Iranian hardliners can frame diplomacy as humiliation; three, that strengthens the very factions least interested in compromise.

Third, rejecting the proposal increases the risk of uncontrolled escalation in a chokepoint that the world economy cannot absorb. One, the Strait of Hormuz handles about one-fifth of global oil and gas exports in peacetime; two, continued naval standoffs and ship interceptions raise insurance, shipping, and energy prices; three, even if the US can intensify pressure, it cannot fully eliminate Iran’s ability to disrupt markets, so the economic downside is global and immediate.

opp_args.thesis: Iran’s proposal is a credible basis for a phased settlement, and Trump’s refusal wastes a rare chance to lock in a broader regional ceasefire.
mechanisms: First, the proposal already contains meaningful concessions. One, Iranian reports say Tehran is willing to dilute part of its highly enriched uranium and transfer the rest to a third country; two, it is willing to suspend enrichment, even if for less than the US wants; three, that is materially better than open-ended confrontation and can be verified over time.

Second, a phased deal is more durable than a maximalist one-shot bargain. One, it starts with ending hostilities and maritime security, which reduces immediate risk; two, it then moves to nuclear and proxy issues once trust and compliance mechanisms exist; three, this mirrors how successful arms-control deals usually work, because sequencing lowers the political cost of compromise.

Third, Trump’s rejection weakens US leverage rather than strengthening it. One, if Iran concludes diplomacy is pointless, it has less reason to restrain attacks on shipping or regional partners; two, the US then has to choose between endless coercion and another war it may not want; three, that makes the rejection look like performative toughness rather than effective statecraft.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercive leverage is best preserved by refusing to concede first, or whether that rigidity simply locks both sides into escalation. The pro side wins if you think Iran’s current leverage must be broken before any durable deal; the opposition wins if you think the US is demanding conditions Iran cannot politically or strategically accept, making phased compromise the only realistic route.

THBT the US should prioritize sanctions relief before nuclear concessions in negotiations with Iran
THP a world where the Strait of Hormuz is reopened only after a comprehensive regional peace deal
THBT maximalist demands in nuclear negotiations do more harm than good
TH, as Trump, would maintain economic pressure rather than accept a phased ceasefire with Iran
