cards.title: Bosnia’s Real Reconciliation Is Economic Integration, Not Elite Truth-Commissions
cards.region: Bosnia and Herzegovina / EU / United States / Balkans
cards.background: Bosnia and Herzegovina emerged from the 1992-95 Bosnian War, which killed about 100,000 people and included the Srebrenica genocide, under the 1995 Dayton Agreement. The country remains split between the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, with separate political and social institutions; the ICTY indicted 161 people and secured 90 convictions. In 2025, Bosnia lost more than 108 million euros in EU funds for missing reform deadlines and could lose another 374 million euros if conditions are not met by December. The article argues that despite political deadlock, Bosnia has sustained roughly 3% average annual growth over the past decade, with dense cross-entity economic ties, 87% of citizens reporting contact with other ethnic groups, and 24% reporting daily contact.

prop_args.thesis: International postconflict policy in Bosnia should prioritize economic interdependence over elite-driven constitutional and truth-justice benchmarks, because shared material stakes are what actually lock in peace.
mechanisms: First, economic interdependence creates a material veto against renewed violence. This is because (1) firms, workers, and municipalities across ethnic lines become dependent on stable borders and functioning institutions, (2) conflict would immediately destroy supply chains, jobs, and investment, and (3) people with assets in mixed markets have a direct incentive to punish nationalist escalation.

Second, cross-entity commerce produces everyday contact that changes social attitudes more reliably than formal reconciliation rituals. Three reasons: one, 87 percent of Bosnians report contact with other ethnic groups and 24 percent daily contact; two, regular contact is associated with trust rising from 22 percent to 47 percent; three, repeated low-stakes cooperation in workplaces and services normalizes coexistence faster than symbolic apologies from elites.

Third, centering economic integration improves policy effectiveness because it rewards the institutions that are already sustaining peace. This matters because (1) Bosnia has continued growing at roughly 3 percent annually despite political crises, (2) joint assets like Elektroprenos BiH and cross-entity employers like Bingo already link communities, and (3) donor money tied only to constitutional reform can miss the actual drivers of stability and misallocate scarce resources.

opp_args.thesis: Economic integration is not a substitute for transitional justice, because without accountability and political reform it can coexist with unresolved grievance, elite manipulation, and fragile peace.
mechanisms: First, material interdependence can be captured by the same nationalist elites who sustain division. One, Dodik and other leaders can profit from cross-entity business while still threatening secession; two, economic ties may enrich connected insiders rather than ordinary citizens; three, if the political order remains discriminatory, commerce does not remove the underlying legitimacy crisis.

Second, focusing on economics alone underestimates the importance of law, memory, and institutional inclusion. One, Bosnia still has ethnically segregated media, education, and parties; two, Dayton bars non-Bosniak/Croat/Serb citizens from some offices and the European Court of Human Rights ruled this discriminatory in 2009; three, unresolved exclusion can keep conflict latent even if trade continues.

Third, donor conditionality on governance and rights is still necessary because it prevents peace from becoming mere frozen coexistence. One, Bosnia lost 108 million euros in 2025 and risks 374 million more, showing leverage exists; two, without pressure, elites have little reason to reform constitutional deadlock; three, transitional justice aims not just to stop war but to build a legitimate political order.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether peace means the absence of violence or the presence of legitimate reconciliation. Prop has the structural advantage on immediate stability because economic ties already exist and create self-enforcing incentives against conflict, while Opp is stronger on long-run justice and institutional legitimacy; the round turns on whether you prioritize durable coexistence or formal transformation.
motion_areas: TH, as international donors, would prioritize economic interdependence over truth-and-reconciliation benchmarks in postconflict states
THBT transitional justice frameworks should measure reconciliation through cross-community economic integration
THP a world where postconflict aid is conditioned more on shared economic institutions than on constitutional reform
THBT Bosnia should be treated as a model of economic reconciliation rather than a frozen conflict

cards.title: Europe’s Competitiveness Crisis Forces a Choice Between Higher Taxes and Industrial Renewal
cards.background: Former French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire said Europe needs an urgent economic reset to build a stronger and more competitive economy. In the interview, he argued that companies such as TotalEnergies should not face higher taxes simply because they are benefiting from elevated oil prices. He also warned about far-left extremism in France, with the French presidential election about one year away.

prop_args.thesis: Europe should resist punitive windfall-style taxation on major firms and instead prioritize competitiveness, investment, and industrial capacity.
mechanisms: First, higher taxes on large profitable firms reduce reinvestment and capital formation. This is because (1) firms facing uncertain tax treatment delay long-term projects, (2) retained earnings are a major source of financing for energy, infrastructure, and R&D, and (3) capital is mobile, so firms can shift investment to lower-tax jurisdictions inside or outside Europe.

Second, a competitiveness-first reset improves Europe’s growth base rather than just redistributing existing rents. Three reasons: one, Europe has lagged the US in productivity and scale-up financing, two, energy and industrial firms need large balance sheets to fund the transition and supply security, and three, stronger firms generate more stable employment and tax revenue over time than one-off extraction.

Third, avoiding punitive taxation reduces the risk of policy volatility and populist backlash. This matters because sudden tax raids signal that success will be punished, which discourages entrepreneurship, encourages lobbying and tax avoidance, and can push voters toward anti-establishment parties that promise even more destructive economic policy.

opp_args.thesis: Europe should tax highly profitable firms more aggressively, especially when they benefit from external shocks, because this is efficient, fair, and politically stabilizing.
mechanisms: First, windfall taxation captures unearned gains created by market shocks rather than productive effort. One, oil-price spikes can massively inflate profits without any corresponding innovation, two, taxing those gains does not meaningfully reduce core productive investment if the profits are excess rents, and three, the revenue can be redirected to households and firms facing higher energy costs.

Second, higher taxes can protect social cohesion during periods of inflation and stagnation. One, when ordinary consumers face energy and food price pressure, visible taxation of large energy firms signals fairness, two, it reduces the perception that elites are profiting from crisis, and three, that legitimacy can be crucial for sustaining broader reform packages.

Third, the state can use the revenue to fund the very competitiveness agenda Le Maire wants. One, public investment in grids, industrial policy, and training can crowd in private investment, two, Europe’s problem is often underinvestment rather than overtaxation, and three, if firms are truly benefiting from monopoly-like rents, taxing them is less distortionary than taxing labor or small business.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether Europe’s binding constraint is lack of capital and confidence or lack of redistribution and legitimacy. The pro side wins if the judge prioritizes long-run growth and investment incentives; the opposition wins if they prove the profits are genuine windfalls and that taxing them funds politically necessary public goods without harming real investment.
motion_areas: TH, as the EU, would oppose windfall taxes on major energy companies
THBT European governments should prioritize competitiveness over higher corporate taxation
THP a world where the state refrains from taxing firms that benefit from commodity price spikes

cards.title: Central Bank Gold Hoarding Signals a More Fragmented Global Financial Order
cards.background: The article argues that central banks’ rising purchases and repatriation of gold should be read as a symptom of deglobalization. It notes that emerging-market central banks have more than doubled their gold holdings since the 2008 global financial crisis, and that recent gold-price behavior since the outbreak of the war with Iran has raised questions about this strategy. The core claim is that these moves reflect a more geopolitically fragmented world in which cross-border transactions are becoming harder and more costly.

prop_args.thesis: Rising official gold reserves are a rational hedge against a world where foreign exchange assets, payment systems, and reserve currencies are increasingly weaponized.
mechanisms: First, gold reduces exposure to sanctions and asset freezes. This is because (1) it is a physical reserve asset that cannot be digitally blocked like correspondent banking balances, (2) it can be repatriated into domestic custody to reduce vulnerability to foreign seizure, and (3) it gives central banks an emergency store of value when access to dollars or euros becomes politically conditional.

Second, gold is a portfolio hedge against geopolitical and monetary volatility. Three reasons: one, wars and sanctions raise the probability of reserve-currency disruptions, two, inflation and currency swings make fiat reserves less reliable in crisis, and three, gold historically performs as a non-liability asset when trust in sovereign issuers falls.

Third, the shift toward gold is a warning signal that deglobalization is already raising transaction costs. This matters because reserve diversification is not just a financial choice; it reflects declining confidence in the openness of the international system, which then feeds back into higher risk premia, more fragmented trade finance, and slower cross-border capital flows.

opp_args.thesis: Gold accumulation is mostly a defensive, low-yielding reaction to uncertainty and does not prove that deglobalization will meaningfully reshape the global financial system.
mechanisms: First, gold is an inefficient reserve asset compared with liquid sovereign bonds. One, it pays no interest, two, it creates storage and security costs, and three, central banks still need dollars and euros for intervention, trade settlement, and liquidity management, so gold cannot replace fiat reserves at scale.

Second, the behavior may be cyclical rather than structural. One, central banks often buy gold when real rates, inflation, or war risk spike, two, those conditions can reverse without any permanent break in globalization, and three, a temporary surge in gold demand does not necessarily imply a durable shift in the architecture of international finance.

Third, the market signal may be overstated because reserve managers are still constrained by size and liquidity. One, the global gold market is too small to absorb a wholesale move out of Treasuries, two, most trade and debt contracts remain dollar-denominated, and three, the network effects of existing reserve currencies make rapid de-dollarization or deglobalization unlikely.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether gold buying is a leading indicator of systemic fragmentation or just a hedge against short-term risk. Prop wins if they prove reserve managers are responding to structural sanctions risk and loss of trust in fiat assets; opp wins if they show gold cannot substitute for the liquidity, yield, and network effects of existing reserve currencies.
motion_areas: TH, as emerging-market central banks, would significantly increase gold reserves
THBT states should repatriate their gold reserves from foreign vaults
THP a world where central banks hold more gold and less foreign sovereign debt
THBT de-dollarization is a rational response to geopolitical fragmentation

cards.title: Trump’s China Visit Risks Turning the Iran War Into a U.S.-China Crisis Bargain
cards.background: NPR reports that President Trump is proceeding with a state visit to China even as the war with Iran continues. The article frames the trip as taking place under the shadow of an active regional conflict, implying that U.S.-China diplomacy is now being conducted alongside a major security crisis. No further operational details are provided in the text beyond the fact of the visit and the ongoing war.

prop_args.thesis: Proceeding with the China visit is strategically useful because it creates a diplomatic channel to prevent the Iran war from escalating into a broader great-power confrontation.
mechanisms: First, the visit gives the U.S. a direct venue to signal red lines and reduce miscalculation. This is because (1) China is a major external stakeholder in any Gulf escalation through energy markets and shipping routes, (2) face-to-face summitry allows leaders to clarify intentions faster than public messaging, and (3) crisis periods increase the value of backchannel coordination over symbolic posturing.

Second, it can split China’s incentives away from reflexive anti-U.S. alignment. Three reasons: one, Beijing has strong economic exposure to stable Middle Eastern energy flows, two, China generally prefers predictability in trade and maritime security, and three, a high-level visit can trade limited cooperation on Iran for concessions in other bilateral areas.

Third, keeping diplomacy alive during war preserves escalation control and lowers the risk of a two-front strategic spiral. This matters because a frozen U.S.-China relationship during an active Iran conflict would make every incident more likely to be interpreted as part of a larger containment strategy, whereas engagement creates off-ramps and bargaining space.

opp_args.thesis: The China trip is dangerous because it turns a regional war into leverage politics, encouraging both China and Iran to harden positions and making U.S. diplomacy look weak.
mechanisms: First, the visit signals that the U.S. is distracted and needs Chinese cooperation, which weakens deterrence. One, adversaries read summitry during crisis as dependence, two, China can demand concessions on trade or Taiwan-related issues in exchange for vague help on Iran, and three, Iran can infer that Washington is trying to avoid escalation at almost any cost.

Second, it risks linking unrelated files and creating bargaining spillovers. One, China may use the Iran war to extract economic or strategic concessions from the U.S., two, the U.S. may soften its China posture to secure help on sanctions or shipping, and three, this cross-issue trading can undermine long-term alliance credibility because partners see security as negotiable.

Third, the trip can embolden China to present itself as the responsible power while quietly benefiting from U.S. distraction. One, Beijing can posture as a mediator without paying real costs, two, it can deepen ties with Iran or other anti-U.S. actors under the cover of diplomacy, and three, the U.S. loses the ability to frame the conflict as a clear aggression-response dynamic.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether summit diplomacy during an active war reduces escalation or creates coercive leverage. Prop has the structural advantage if the round is about crisis management, because even modest communication can prevent catastrophic miscalculation; Opp wins if the frame is credibility and bargaining power, since the optics of needing China during war can weaken U.S. deterrence.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would proceed with high-level diplomacy with China during an ongoing regional war
THBT great powers should prioritize summit diplomacy with rivals even during active conflicts involving third states
THP a world where major-power trade and security negotiations continue during wartime

cards.title: Russian Drone Spillover Pushes Latvia to Deepen Joint Air-Defense With Ukraine
cards.background: Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze said Latvia will work with Ukraine and its allies to improve defenses against drones that stray into Latvian territory. The announcement came after two drones crashed in eastern Latvia last week, triggering political fallout and forcing Defense Minister Andris Spruds to resign late on Sunday. Braze made the remarks ahead of the Foreign Affairs Council in Brussels on Monday.

prop_args.thesis: Cross-border drone incidents force frontline NATO states to build integrated, Ukraine-linked air defense systems because isolated national defenses are too slow, too expensive, and too vulnerable to saturation.
mechanisms: First, joint drone defense improves detection and interception speed. This is because (1) drones cross borders in minutes, so a purely national response arrives too late, (2) Ukraine has already accumulated battlefield experience against mass drone attacks, and (3) shared intelligence and sensor networks reduce the time between detection and engagement.

Second, cooperation lowers the cost of defense relative to the threat. Three reasons: one, drones are cheap and can be deployed in large numbers, two, traditional air-defense missiles are far more expensive than the targets they destroy, and three, pooling technology with Ukraine lets Latvia adapt lower-cost counter-drone tools instead of relying only on high-end systems.

Third, this creates a stronger deterrent posture on NATO’s eastern flank. This matters because a visible, coordinated response signals that drone spillovers will not produce political paralysis, it reduces the chance that Russia can exploit ambiguity or deniability, and it helps normalize a forward-defense model for other exposed states in the region.

opp_args.thesis: Deepening drone-defense cooperation with Ukraine risks militarizing border incidents and exposing Latvia to escalation, dependency, and domestic political backlash.
mechanisms: First, closer operational integration can blur the line between defense and co-belligerency. One, Russia can frame shared systems, intelligence, or training as direct NATO involvement, two, that gives Moscow propaganda and escalation leverage, and three, it raises the risk that Latvia becomes a more attractive target for retaliation.

Second, relying on Ukraine can create capability dependency rather than resilience. One, Ukraine’s systems are optimized for wartime conditions, not peacetime border management, two, Latvia may import tactics that are hard to sustain without Ukraine’s scale of mobilization, and three, this can crowd out investment in durable national air-defense infrastructure.

Third, the political shock from drone incidents can produce overreaction and instability. One, the defense minister’s resignation shows how quickly public confidence can collapse, two, governments may respond with symbolic security measures instead of effective ones, and three, that can distort budget priorities away from broader defense needs.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the threat is best understood as a one-off border nuisance or as a structural feature of modern warfare on NATO’s frontier. Prop wins if the round is about practical security adaptation, because the cost asymmetry and speed of drone attacks make cooperation the most efficient response; opp wins if the round is about escalation risk, because any integration with Ukraine can be framed by Russia as a step toward direct confrontation.
motion_areas: TH, as a frontline NATO state, would integrate its air-defense systems with Ukraine’s
THBT European states bordering Russia should prioritize joint counter-drone cooperation with Ukraine
THP a world where NATO states adopt Ukraine-style battlefield air-defense innovation

cards.title: Iran War Accelerates a Gulf Security Realignment as Netanyahu Seeks to Lock In a New Regional Order
cards.background: In an Al Jazeera interview published on 2026-05-11, former Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim Al Thani said the US-Israel war on Iran is part of a long-term Israeli effort to reshape the Middle East. He argued that the most dangerous fallout is the Strait of Hormuz crisis, warned that Iran has weaponised the chokepoint, and called for a unified Gulf defence pact or "Gulf NATO." He also said the war has killed more than 72,500 Palestinians since October 2023, criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza, and argued that Gulf states can no longer rely indefinitely on the US security umbrella as Washington pivots toward Asia.

prop_args.thesis: The Iran war will accelerate a durable Gulf security realignment by forcing regional states to build independent collective defence and diplomacy rather than rely on the US.
mechanisms: First, the war exposes the fragility of the US security umbrella. This is because (1) Washington is increasingly distracted by Asia and China containment, (2) Gulf states see that US protection did not prevent strikes on regional infrastructure, and (3) allies now have to hedge by building their own deterrence instead of assuming automatic American intervention.

Second, the conflict creates a direct incentive for Gulf institutionalization. Three reasons: one, the Strait of Hormuz threat makes energy security a shared survival issue; two, Iranian attacks on Gulf energy, industrial and civilian infrastructure generate common threat perceptions across rival Gulf monarchies; three, a formal pact lowers coordination costs for intelligence-sharing, missile defence, and crisis response.

Third, the war weakens the political feasibility of ad hoc diplomacy and pushes states toward bloc politics. This matters because once leaders and publics conclude that fragmented bilateral channels failed to prevent escalation, they prefer a structured alliance architecture that can bargain collectively with Iran, the US, Turkiye, Pakistan, and Egypt.

opp_args.thesis: The war will not produce a stable new order; it will deepen fragmentation because Gulf states have incompatible threat perceptions and cannot sustain a real collective defence bloc.
mechanisms: First, the Gulf is too divided for a meaningful NATO-style pact. One, states differ on whether Iran, Israel, or domestic instability is the primary threat; two, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, and others have competing foreign policy priorities; three, alliance commitments become unreliable when members fear being dragged into each other’s escalations.

Second, the war incentivizes unilateral hedging rather than collective action. One, smaller states will seek separate deals with the US, China, Turkiye, or Iran to maximize regime security; two, energy exporters prefer flexibility over binding military obligations; three, any formal bloc risks becoming symbolic because members will free-ride on others’ deterrence.

Third, escalation around Hormuz is more likely to produce economic coercion than institutional reform. One, Iran can threaten shipping without needing to occupy territory; two, Gulf states will prioritize short-term de-escalation to protect oil flows; three, once the immediate crisis passes, the political will for deep integration usually collapses.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether shared vulnerability translates into durable institutional cooperation or just temporary crisis management. Prop wins if the war permanently changes Gulf threat perception and makes self-help unavoidable; opp wins if intra-Gulf mistrust and divergent interests prevent any real collective security architecture from forming.

cards.title: Taiwan’s Civilian Militarisation Signals a Shift From Deterrence to Societal Preparedness Ahead of Trump-Xi Bargaining
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported that Taiwanese civilians were increasingly enrolling in self-defence courses amid fears that China could one day use force to seize the island. The report came just days before a scheduled meeting between Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, with some Taiwanese residents worrying that Taiwan’s future could be discussed in the talks. The article reflects heightened uncertainty over cross-strait security and the possibility of Taiwan being treated as a bargaining issue in US-China diplomacy.

prop_args.thesis: Civilian self-defence training is a rational and stabilising response because it raises Taiwan’s resilience, strengthens deterrence, and reduces the chance that coercion succeeds quickly.
mechanisms: First, it improves societal resilience in the event of limited coercion or a grey-zone campaign. This is because (1) civilians learn basic protection, evacuation, and emergency response skills, (2) that reduces panic and makes it harder for an attacker to create rapid psychological collapse, and (3) a population that can organize locally buys time for the state and military to respond.

Second, it strengthens deterrence by signaling that Taiwan is not a passive target. Three reasons: one, a society willing to train for resistance raises the expected cost of occupation; two, it complicates any Chinese assumption of a quick, low-cost takeover; three, it communicates domestic resolve to both Beijing and Washington, making abandonment less likely.

Third, it creates strategic depth beyond formal military capacity. This matters because Taiwan cannot rely only on conventional force asymmetry; if civilians can sustain continuity of governance, logistics, and local defense, then any invasion becomes longer, costlier, and politically harder to justify internationally.

opp_args.thesis: Civilian self-defence training can be counterproductive because it normalizes fear, increases escalation risks, and may be used as a substitute for serious state-level deterrence.
mechanisms: First, it can fuel panic and social militarisation. One, constant preparation for invasion can make the public more anxious and less economically confident; two, that anxiety can damage investment and social cohesion; three, it may create a self-fulfilling security spiral where each side interprets the other’s actions as hostile.

Second, it may provoke China or harden its narrative. One, Beijing can frame civilian training as proof that Taiwan is moving toward permanent separation; two, that gives hawks in China more ammunition for coercive rhetoric or military drills; three, it reduces diplomatic space by making compromise look weaker domestically on both sides.

Third, it risks substituting symbolism for real deterrence. One, self-defence classes do not solve Taiwan’s core vulnerabilities in air defence, missiles, cyber, or command-and-control; two, governments may overstate preparedness to avoid making hard procurement or alliance decisions; three, that leaves Taiwan with a false sense of security while the strategic balance remains unchanged.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether civilian preparedness meaningfully changes the cost-benefit calculation for China or merely creates symbolism. Prop wins if the round is about resilience and deterrence under uncertainty; Opp wins if they prove the training is mostly psychological theatre that either escalates tensions or distracts from real military capability.
motion_areas: TH, as Taiwan, would encourage widespread civilian self-defence training
THBT small states facing existential threats should militarise civilian preparedness
THP a world where societies under threat invest heavily in civilian resistance training

cards.title: US Troop Presence in Lithuania Becomes a Test of NATO Deterrence vs Escalation Risk
cards.region: Lithuania / United States / Russia / European Union
cards.background: Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said in a Bloomberg interview on Monday that Vilnius welcomes US troops "wherever they are" in Europe, while arguing that their deterrent value is greater the closer they are to Russia. His comments came ahead of the Foreign Affairs Council in Brussels, where European security and NATO posture were likely to be discussed. The statement reflects ongoing concern in the Baltic states about Russian aggression and the credibility of NATO's eastern flank.

prop_args.thesis: Forward-deploying US troops in Lithuania strengthens deterrence by making any Russian attack immediately costly and politically harder to ignore.
mechanisms: First, closer troop placement improves deterrence credibility. This is because (1) it reduces response time in the event of a Russian incursion, (2) it creates a visible tripwire that signals automatic US involvement, and (3) it makes it harder for Moscow to believe NATO would delay or split over a crisis.

Second, it reassures frontline allies and stabilizes the eastern flank. Three reasons: one, Baltic states are more likely to invest in defense and coordination when they trust the US security guarantee; two, domestic publics in exposed states are less likely to panic or hedge toward accommodation with Russia; three, allied cohesion improves when the most vulnerable members see concrete commitment rather than abstract promises.

Third, the strategic payoff is disproportionate to the troop numbers involved. This matters because a relatively small US presence can generate outsized deterrent effects by signaling alliance resolve, raising the expected cost of aggression, and forcing Russia to plan around a more unified NATO response.

opp_args.thesis: Placing US troops closer to Russia can increase escalation risk and reduce strategic flexibility, making Europe less secure in a crisis.
mechanisms: First, forward deployment can be read by Russia as offensive encirclement rather than defensive reassurance. One, this encourages reciprocal military buildup and more aggressive Russian posturing; two, it narrows diplomatic off-ramps because both sides become more invested in not appearing weak; three, it increases the chance that routine incidents are misread as preparation for attack.

Second, it creates a tripwire that may lock the US into conflict on unfavorable terms. One, if troops are stationed near the border, Washington faces stronger pressure to respond militarily to any incident; two, that reduces room for de-escalation or bargaining in a fast-moving crisis; three, it can turn local provocations into alliance-wide confrontation.

Third, it may crowd out broader European burden-sharing and defense planning. One, frontline states may over-rely on US protection instead of building autonomous capabilities; two, Western European states may treat the eastern flank as a US problem rather than a collective one; three, security policy becomes more dependent on US domestic politics, which is unstable over time.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether proximity increases deterrence more than it increases escalation risk. Prop wins if the round is about credibility and alliance reassurance in the shadow of Russian aggression; opp wins if the judge prioritizes crisis stability and the danger of accidental or forced escalation.
motion_areas: TH, as NATO, would permanently station more US troops in Lithuania
THBT frontline states should host greater numbers of US troops near Russia
THP a world where NATO maintains a stronger forward military presence in Eastern Europe

cards.title: US-Iran Standoff Over Hormuz Keeps War Alive and Threatens Global Energy Shock
cards.region: Iran / US / Middle East (Strait of Hormuz)
cards.background: Iran’s foreign ministry said on 11 May 2026 that the US was making “unreasonable” and “one-sided” demands in talks aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, as a fragile ceasefire held. Iran said it had sent a counterproposal via Pakistan, including an end to the war, lifting the blockade on Iranian ports, releasing frozen assets, and guaranteeing safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Donald Trump called Iran’s response “totally unacceptable,” while Brent crude rose 4.65 percent to $99.95 a barrel and WTI rose just over 4 percent to $105.50 amid fears of supply disruption.

prop_args.thesis: Iran’s hard line is rational because it uses control over Hormuz and regional energy flows to force the US into a settlement that ends the war on terms Tehran can survive.
mechanisms: First, Iran’s leverage is structural, not rhetorical. This is because (1) the Strait of Hormuz is the chokepoint for a huge share of Gulf oil and shipping, (2) even the threat of disruption immediately moved Brent by 4.65 percent and WTI by over 4 percent, and (3) that price shock hits the US, Europe, and Asian importers faster than it hits Iran, so Tehran can impose costs without matching US military reach.

Second, maximalist bargaining can improve Iran’s end-state by raising the price of escalation for Washington. Three reasons: one, the US has to weigh domestic inflation and energy prices; two, allies like the UK and France are already worried enough to coordinate naval protection, showing the coalition burden is real; three, if Iran signals it can reopen or close Hormuz, it turns a military conflict into a broader economic hostage situation that incentivizes compromise.

Third, the proposal is framed as legitimacy politics, not just coercion. This matters because Iran is tying any deal to ending the war, unblocking ports, and releasing frozen assets, which lets it present itself as defending sovereignty rather than surrendering; that helps maintain domestic cohesion and regional deterrence while avoiding the appearance of capitulation.

prop_args.thesis: European involvement and maritime protection efforts strengthen Iran’s case that the conflict is becoming an internationalized security crisis, making a negotiated regional settlement more attractive than continued military pressure.
mechanisms: First, the more external actors enter the theater, the harder it becomes for the US to control escalation. One, the UK and France are hosting multinational defense-minister talks to restore trade flows; two, a coalition of more than 50 countries is being assembled; three, Iran can portray this as foreign intervention, which increases the political cost of continued pressure and complicates coalition unity.

Second, the war is already producing spillover costs that no side can fully contain. Three reasons: one, the analyst quoted in the article says the real casualty is the international economy and Gulf populations; two, the price spike shows immediate global transmission; three, any intervention in Hormuz risks further complications, so a ceasefire-plus-deconfliction deal is the only stable equilibrium.

Third, Iran’s demands on assets and shipping are the kind of concrete concessions that can be traded in diplomacy. This matters because frozen assets, blockade relief, and maritime guarantees are all reversible policy tools, so the US can save face by trading limited sanctions relief for de-escalation rather than pursuing an open-ended war.

opp_args.thesis: Iran’s demands are too expansive and coercive, so the US is right to reject them because conceding would reward aggression and weaken deterrence.
mechanisms: First, accepting Iran’s proposal would create a dangerous precedent. One, it would show that threatening Hormuz can extract sanctions relief and asset releases; two, it would incentivize future brinkmanship by Iran and other regional actors; three, it would undermine the credibility of US red lines on nuclear and military behavior.

Second, the US cannot trade away core security objectives for temporary calm. One, Trump has already said the US will not allow Iran to reach enriched uranium; two, Iran’s proposal appears to bundle war termination with strategic concessions, which Washington may read as preserving Iran’s long-term military capacity; three, if the US gives in now, it may face a stronger Iran later with more resources and legitimacy.

Third, a hard line may be necessary to protect allies and keep shipping open. One, European warship deployments show partners want active maritime security rather than accommodation; two, if the US signals weakness, Gulf states may doubt its willingness to defend the passage; three, deterrence is more credible when coercive threats are met with resistance, not bargaining.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercive leverage produces a stable bargain or simply rewards escalation. Prop wins if you think Hormuz gives Iran asymmetric economic power that the US cannot ignore; opp wins if you think conceding under threat destroys deterrence and invites repeat crises.

THBT states should prioritize energy security over punitive sanctions in wartime negotiations
THP a world where regional chokepoints can be used as bargaining leverage in peace talks

cards.title: Trump 2.0 Turns US Cities Into a Tourism and Business Boycott Target for Canadians
cards.region: Canada / US border towns and metro areas
cards.background: Researchers at the University of Toronto used cell-phone activity data to track Canadian visits to US metro areas between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2026. They found a year-over-year median decline of about 42% in Canadian visits to US metropolitan areas, compared with a roughly 25% decline in official border-crossing data. The biggest drops were in border towns and also in major destinations such as New York, New Hampshire, Vermont, Las Vegas, Walt Disney World, Florida winter-recreation areas, and business hubs like San Francisco, Houston, and Grand Rapids, Michigan. The researchers linked the decline to Trump administration immigration crackdowns, tariffs on Canadian goods including vehicles, and broader anger over threats to make Canada the “51st state.”

prop_args.thesis: Trump-era border hostility and tariffs are economically self-defeating because they convert Canada from a high-value nearby market into a partial boycott, hitting US border economies, tourism, and cross-border business travel at once.
mechanisms: First, the policy shock changes Canadian consumer behavior away from discretionary travel. This is because (1) Canadians can easily substitute US trips with domestic or third-country destinations, (2) the 42% median decline shows the effect is not marginal but behaviorally large, and (3) the decline is concentrated in metro areas and tourist hubs, meaning the lost spending is exactly the kind of high-margin tourism revenue cities depend on.

Second, the damage is amplified in border and integrated industrial regions. Three reasons: one, towns reliant on Canadian foot traffic lose hotel, retail, and restaurant demand immediately; two, places like Grand Rapids lose repeated work-related travel tied to the auto supply chain; three, reduced business travel weakens the dense cross-border networks that support trade, investment, and just-in-time production.

Third, the policy creates a broader confidence shock that outlasts the current administration. This matters because (1) once firms and households learn the US is politically volatile, they diversify away from US destinations and supply chains, (2) return migration and reduced business travel can permanently thin cross-border ties, and (3) the official 25% border-crossing decline understates the real loss, so the economic harm is likely bigger than policymakers admit.

opp_args.thesis: The decline is real but overstated as a policy failure, because it is partly measurement noise and the US can absorb the lost Canadian demand without major macroeconomic damage.
mechanisms: First, the 42% figure is not a clean measure of tourism alone. One, the cell-phone tool also captures freight traffic and Canadians temporarily living in the US, so the decline may reflect return migration or data artifacts rather than pure consumer boycott; two, official border-crossing data shows a smaller 25% decline, suggesting the headline number overstates the true tourism shock; three, metro-level declines do not automatically translate into national economic pain.

Second, the US has a large enough domestic and international market to replace Canadian visitors. One, cities like Las Vegas, Orlando, and New York have diversified tourist bases far beyond Canada; two, border towns are economically exposed but are a narrow slice of the US economy; three, businesses can reorient marketing toward domestic travelers or other foreign tourists over time.

Third, some of the decline may be a rational reallocation rather than a permanent boycott. One, if Canadians are avoiding the US because of tariffs or enforcement, that is a political response that can reverse with policy changes; two, firms and households may simply be delaying travel during uncertainty rather than abandoning it; three, temporary demand shifts are less damaging than structural trade collapse and may not justify strong conclusions about long-run harm.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the Canadian decline is a temporary measurement artifact or a durable loss of high-value cross-border demand. Prop wins if it proves the shock is concentrated in integrated border and business ecosystems, because those sectors are hardest to replace and most sensitive to trust; Opp wins only if it can show the US can quickly substitute away the lost spending and that the data exaggerates the true behavioral change.

cards.title: Democratic Middle-Class Tax Cuts Risk Cementing a Smaller, Weaker Welfare State
cards.background: After the 2024 election, Democrats have been debating how to respond to Republican ownership of tax cuts and Trump’s economic messaging. A prominent proposal from Sen. Chris Van Hollen would cut taxes for Americans earning up to $80,500 ($161,000 for married couples) and fund the estimated $1.6tn 10-year cost with a new surtax on Americans making more than $1m. Under Penn-Wharton estimates cited in the piece, middle-income households in the 40th to 80th percentile would save about $1,500 in 2026, while taxpayers in the top 0.1% would pay an average of $1.2m more.

prop_args.thesis: Democrats should pursue middle-class tax cuts because they are the fastest way to rebuild electoral credibility and make redistribution politically durable.
mechanisms: First, the policy directly targets the median voter and restores trust in Democrats as competent economic managers. This is because (1) voters already perceive Republicans as stronger on taxes and household finances, (2) a visible $1,500 annual tax cut is easy to understand and campaign on, and (3) winning back the middle class is a prerequisite for passing any larger social-democratic agenda later.

Second, the proposal shifts the tax debate onto terrain where Democrats can split the Republican coalition. Three reasons: one, it forces Republicans to defend tax cuts that disproportionately benefited the rich under Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act; two, it reframes tax relief as a family issue rather than an anti-government ideology; three, it helps Democrats reclaim the symbolic ownership of 'tax cuts' without abandoning progressive financing.

Third, even if it is not a full welfare-state solution, it still improves disposable income for ordinary households in the short run. This matters because (1) families can use the extra cash immediately on rent, food, debt, or childcare, (2) the political salience of direct tax relief is much higher than abstract promises of future transfers, and (3) small but broad gains can reduce the sense that the state only helps elites or the poor.

opp_args.thesis: Middle-class tax cuts are a trap because they consume political capital while shrinking the fiscal space needed for real redistribution and public services.
mechanisms: First, they normalize the idea that the state should return money rather than build capacity. One, that makes it harder to justify future tax increases on the wealthy; two, it entrenches anti-tax politics even when the revenue is needed for health, care, and infrastructure; three, it shifts the party from structural reform to consumer-style handouts.

Second, they are a low-efficiency way to reduce inequality compared with transfers and services. One, the article cites World Bank and Paris School of Economics research that transfers account for 90% of inequality reduction while taxes account for only 10%; two, a $1,500 tax cut is roughly offset by Americans' high out-of-pocket health costs, so the net welfare gain is small; three, without expanded public provision, the underlying drivers of inequality remain untouched.

Third, the policy weakens the case for taxing wealth and capital properly. One, if Democrats spend their credibility on a middle-class tax cut, they have less room to sell harder reforms like taxing unrealized gains or ending inheritance loopholes; two, the very rich still accumulate wealth through capital gains and estate planning, so the real revenue base remains under-taxed; three, the result is a more permanent underfunding of the state, which locks in the US's low-tax, low-transfer equilibrium.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term electoral appeal and long-term state capacity. The opposition wins if the round is about whether Democrats should maximize the chance of a quick political rebound; the proposition wins if the round is about whether policy should actually reduce inequality and fund a durable social contract.

cards.title: Nazi-Looted Art Discovery Reopens Europe’s Unfinished Restitution Wars
cards.background: A painting titled Portrait of a Young Girl by Dutch artist Toon Kelder was identified by art detective Arthur Brand as likely having been looted by the Nazis from Jewish dealer Jacques Goudstikker in 1940. The work reportedly hung for decades in the home of descendants of Hendrik Seyffardt, a Dutch general who led a Waffen-SS volunteer unit on the eastern front and was assassinated in 1943. Goudstikker died while fleeing the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands, leaving behind a collection of more than 1,000 paintings; Brand says the work matches a lot number from a 1940 auction of the looted collection and could potentially still be sold because the statute of limitations on theft has expired.

prop_args.thesis: Public identification and restitution of Nazi-looted art is necessary to enforce historical justice and prevent stolen cultural property from being normalized through private possession.
mechanisms: First, restitution restores the property rights of victims’ heirs and prevents the legal system from laundering wartime theft into ordinary ownership. This is because (1) Nazi looting was not a normal market transaction but coercive seizure under occupation, (2) private retention decades later compounds the original crime by converting stolen goods into family assets, and (3) public exposure creates pressure on holders who would otherwise rely on silence and time to keep the work.

Second, disclosure deters future concealment of looted assets by making possession reputationally costly. Three reasons: one, families and institutions are less likely to hide provenance when they know journalists, detectives, and claimants can trace works through labels, auction records, and archival numbers; two, it raises the expected cost of non-return because public shame and legal scrutiny increase; three, it signals that even old thefts remain morally and politically salient, reducing incentives to wait out statutes of limitation.

Third, restitution strengthens the broader international norm that cultural property stolen in atrocity contexts should be returned, not monetized. This matters because (1) Holocaust-era looting is a template case for post-conflict justice, (2) if Europe tolerates these claims being buried in private homes, it weakens confidence in museums, auction houses, and art markets worldwide, and (3) returning the work is a low-cost but high-symbolic-value act that acknowledges the destruction of Jewish life and property under the Nazis.

opp_args.thesis: Aggressive public restitution campaigns can create legal uncertainty and overreach, punishing descendants who may not have known the provenance and destabilizing art ownership norms.
mechanisms: First, retrospective claims are hard to adjudicate cleanly because evidence decays over 80 years. One, records are incomplete and auction trails are fragmented, so innocent purchasers can be swept into disputes; two, heirs may genuinely lack knowledge of wartime provenance, making moral blame weaker than the original theft; three, broad public pressure can force settlements before courts establish ownership with confidence.

Second, expanding restitution through media exposure can chill legitimate art markets and private collecting. One, buyers face higher due-diligence costs and greater risk of latent claims; two, families may avoid preserving inherited works for fear of retroactive seizure; three, uncertainty can reduce liquidity and discourage loans, exhibitions, and conservation investments.

Third, statute-of-limitations rules exist to create finality, and overriding them selectively can undermine rule-of-law predictability. One, if old claims are reopened whenever a detective finds a trace, ownership never truly settles; two, selective moral exceptions privilege high-profile cases over equally valid but less visible disputes; three, governments may be pressured into symbolic restitution even where compensation, archival acknowledgment, or shared custody would better balance competing interests.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between moral clarity and legal finality: Prop has the stronger structural claim because the original taking was an atrocity, so time does not cleanse title in the same way it would for ordinary property. Opp’s best point is administrability, but that is weaker where the evidence is unusually specific and the harm is the continued possession of stolen Holocaust-era art.

cards.title: Global AI Governance Fails Because States Disagree on Whether AI Is a Sectoral Tool or Civilizational Power Shift
cards.background: The article argues that international AI governance remains weak because states do not share a common definition of AI or a common view of how fast it will transform politics and the economy. It notes that AI summit commitments in India were voluntary, enforcement of past Seoul AI Summit commitments has been shaky, and global debates remain fractured. The piece highlights that the U.S. and China account for roughly 90% of global AI compute and most leading models, while many other states remain dependent on them for access to frontier capabilities.

prop_args.thesis: Global AI coordination fails because states have incompatible epistemics about both the pace of AI development and their own dependence on foreign AI ecosystems.
mechanisms: First, states cannot agree on the object of regulation. This is because (1) some governments mean ChatGPT-style large language models, (2) others mean AGI or superintelligence, and (3) others mean ordinary machine-learning systems, so negotiations collapse before they even reach substantive trade-offs.

Second, states disagree on the time horizon of risk, which produces incompatible policy priorities. Three reasons: one, actors who expect rapid civilizational transformation prioritize frontier-model testing, cyber risk, and concentration of power; two, actors who expect slower diffusion prioritize labor disruption, cultural harms, and domestic industrial policy; three, these different threat models generate different legal language and different summit agendas, making common rules impossible.

Third, dependency structure creates incentives against multilateralism. This matters because (1) the U.S. and China control most compute and leading models, so they have little reason to hand authority to international bodies; (2) smaller states that want access are incentivized to bandwagon with one bloc rather than build universal rules; and (3) states that lack domestic capacity cannot credibly enforce global standards, so coordination efforts become symbolic rather than binding.

opp_args.thesis: Despite definitional disagreement, AI governance can still emerge through narrow, interest-based coalitions and functional regulation.
mechanisms: First, governments do not need a shared philosophy of AI to regulate concrete harms. One, they can agree on specific issues like model safety testing, cyber misuse, deepfakes, data protection, and export controls; two, these are observable policy targets even if states disagree on AGI; three, many past regimes began with partial consensus rather than total conceptual agreement.

Second, power asymmetry can actually facilitate coordination. One, the U.S. and China dominate compute and model development, so bilateral or club-based standards can set de facto global norms; two, smaller states often follow market access and compliance incentives; three, once major firms adopt common safety or reporting rules, international governance can spread through private-sector standardization even without universal agreement.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether epistemic disagreement is a hard barrier or just a coordination cost. Prop wins if the round is about why multilateral institutions fail to produce binding rules; opp wins if the judge prefers a narrower view of governance where partial, bilateral, or industry-led standards are enough to count as coordination.

TH, as a medium-sized state, would prioritize bilateral AI deals over multilateral AI regulation
THP a world where frontier AI development is governed by a small club of major powers rather than universal institutions
THBT developing countries should bandwagon with U.S. or Chinese AI ecosystems rather than pursue independent AI governance

cards.title: Trump’s Immigration Agenda Moves From Miller’s Mass-Deportation Model Toward a More Targeted, Politically Safer Enforcement Strategy
cards.background: The article describes an internal shift in the Trump administration’s second-term immigration policy away from Stephen Miller’s maximalist enforcement agenda. Trump reversed a planned roughly 50 percent cut to seasonal-worker visas after the Minneapolis killings, and later replaced Miller’s preferred DHS approach with a more conventional targeted-enforcement model under Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE veteran Tom Homan. ICE arrests fell from about 36,000 in January to about 30,000 in March, while detainee numbers dropped from roughly 70,000 in late January to about 60,000 by late April. Miller had previously driven a $175 billion immigration-enforcement package, a goal of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, and a push to add 12,000 ICE officers and agents.

prop_args.thesis: Trump’s retreat from Miller-style immigration hardball is politically rational because it reduces backlash, restores administrative competence, and preserves the issue as an electoral asset rather than a liability.
mechanisms: First, it lowers the political salience of visibly harsh enforcement. This is because (1) family-separation-style optics and street clashes create bipartisan outrage, (2) that outrage can rapidly flip immigration from a strength into a weakness, and (3) once the issue becomes associated with chaos rather than control, the president loses the ability to claim competence.

Second, it improves operational effectiveness by shifting from quota-driven spectacle to targeted enforcement. Three reasons: one, prioritizing immigrants with criminal records or pending orders concentrates resources on higher-value removals; two, reducing drama lowers resistance from local communities and employers; three, slower but steadier enforcement avoids the high dropout, training, and coordination problems created by Miller’s rushed expansion.

Third, it protects the broader governing coalition by accommodating business and labor-market pressures. This matters because (1) hospitality, construction, and landscaping employers depend on seasonal labor, (2) abrupt visa cuts create immediate shortages and price shocks, and (3) when the White House walks back extreme restrictions, it signals to markets and donors that policy will not be held hostage to ideological purity.

opp_args.thesis: Scaling back Miller’s agenda weakens deterrence, emboldens migrants and activists, and signals that the administration is unwilling to sustain the level of coercion needed to achieve mass deportation.
mechanisms: First, softer enforcement reduces deterrence. One, if arrests fall from a mass-arrest model to targeted enforcement, fewer people perceive a credible threat of removal; two, once migrants believe the state is selective rather than relentless, the expected payoff of entering or staying illegally rises; three, that makes future surges more likely and raises the long-run enforcement burden.

Second, it fractures the internal enforcement coalition. One, Miller’s model depends on aggressive coordination across DHS, ICE, CBP, and the White House; two, replacing him with law-enforcement managers who prefer caution creates bureaucratic drift and mixed signals; three, mixed signals reduce morale among hardliners and encourage career officials to slow-walk implementation.

Third, it abandons the political opportunity to lock in a durable anti-immigration realignment. One, mass enforcement can mobilize the base and force Democrats onto the defensive; two, retreating after backlash teaches opponents that protests work; three, if the administration does not keep escalating, it loses the chance to normalize a much stricter immigration regime.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term political damage and long-term deterrence. Prop wins if the round is about governability and electoral sustainability; opp wins if you believe only maximal coercion can create durable migration deterrence and that any retreat signals weakness.

THBT governments should reverse hardline immigration policies when they create visible political backlash
THP a world where immigration enforcement is run by career law-enforcement officials rather than political ideologues

cards.title: UK Nationalises British Steel to Prevent Industrial Collapse and Foreign Asset Exit
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, Prime Minister Keir Starmer said the UK government would bring forward legislation this week to give it powers to take full ownership of British Steel, subject to a public interest test. The announcement follows the government seizing control of British Steel’s Scunthorpe steelworks from its Chinese owner Jingye in April 2025 to stop the possible closure of the site’s blast furnaces. Starmer said talks with Jingye had failed to produce a commercial sale, making public ownership the next step.

prop_args.thesis: Nationalisation is justified because steel is a strategic industrial input where market failure and foreign ownership create unacceptable risks to jobs, supply chains, and national resilience.
mechanisms: First, public ownership prevents a sudden collapse of a strategically important firm. This is because (1) steel is an upstream input for construction, defence, transport, and infrastructure, (2) private owners facing losses have incentives to shut blast furnaces quickly rather than absorb long-term losses, and (3) once heavy industrial capacity is lost, it is extremely expensive and slow to rebuild.

Second, nationalisation protects domestic employment and the wider local economy. Three reasons: one, Scunthorpe jobs are directly tied to the plant; two, supplier and service firms depend on the steelworks, so closure multiplies unemployment beyond the site itself; three, preserving the plant avoids a regional shock that would otherwise hit tax revenues, housing demand, and local public services.

Third, state ownership secures bargaining power over a critical asset that foreign owners may not treat as a national priority. This matters because the government can keep production running while restructuring the business, preventing a fire-sale closure and ensuring the UK retains sovereign control over a sector with national security and industrial policy implications.

opp_args.thesis: Nationalisation is a costly bailout that entrenches inefficiency, politicises industrial policy, and sets a precedent for state rescue of failing firms.
mechanisms: First, state ownership weakens incentives to innovate and cut costs. One, managers under public ownership are less exposed to profit-and-loss discipline; two, political pressure often keeps uncompetitive plants open longer than economically justified; three, this can lock in low productivity and delay necessary restructuring.

Second, it imposes fiscal costs and opportunity costs on taxpayers. One, the government must cover operating losses, capital upgrades, and environmental compliance; two, those funds could otherwise support higher-return investments like skills, infrastructure, or new industries; three, repeated bailouts create moral hazard by signalling that politically important firms will be rescued regardless of performance.

Third, it can deter future foreign investment and worsen UK credibility on property rights. One, investors may fear that strategic assets can be taken over when politically convenient; two, this increases perceived sovereign risk and raises the cost of capital; three, it may reduce the willingness of international firms to invest in UK manufacturing or enter joint ventures.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether British Steel is a normal failing firm or a strategic asset with irreversible spillovers if it closes. Prop wins if the round prioritises industrial resilience and local economic devastation; opp wins if the round prioritises long-run efficiency, fiscal discipline, and the precedent set for state intervention.
motion_areas: TH, as the UK government, would nationalise British Steel
THBT governments should nationalise strategically important failing industries
THP a world where states can take over critical industrial assets from foreign owners

cards.title: Starmer Bets on EU Re-Engagement and Steel Nationalisation to Rescue Labour’s Economic Credibility
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, Keir Starmer used a speech amid renewed Labour leadership speculation to argue that incremental change was no longer enough and that his government needed a bigger economic reset. He announced legislation would be brought forward this week to give the government powers, subject to a public interest test, to take full public ownership of British Steel after commercial sale talks in Scunthorpe failed. He also said Labour would set a new direction with the EU at the next summit, including an ambitious youth experience scheme and deeper economic, trade, and defence cooperation.

prop_args.thesis: Starmer’s shift toward industrial intervention and closer EU ties is the right economic response to Britain’s stagnation because it restores strategic capacity, lowers trade frictions, and signals a break from failed Brexit-era policy.
mechanisms: First, nationalising British Steel protects a strategic input that private markets have failed to secure. This is because (1) steel is a core upstream industry for defence, infrastructure, and manufacturing, (2) a failed commercial sale in Scunthorpe shows the asset is not being allocated efficiently by the market, and (3) public ownership prevents a disorderly collapse that would destroy skilled jobs and local supply chains.

Second, rebuilding ties with the EU improves growth by reducing post-Brexit friction. Three reasons: one, closer alignment can cut trade barriers for exporters and importers, two, a youth mobility scheme and restored Erasmus-style links improve labour-market matching and human capital, and three, stronger cooperation with Europe supports investment confidence by making Britain look less isolated and more predictable.

Third, this strategy is politically and economically necessary because the status quo has already failed to deliver on Brexit promises. This matters because if voters believe Brexit made Britain poorer and weaker, then a government that refuses to adapt looks captured by ideology rather than focused on living standards, which depresses business confidence and weakens long-run growth.

opp_args.thesis: Starmer’s interventionist turn risks worsening Britain’s economic problems by increasing state exposure, politicising industry, and offering symbolic Europe policy rather than material growth.
mechanisms: First, nationalising British Steel may create a costly precedent for state bailouts. One, it shifts commercial risk onto taxpayers if the sector remains uncompetitive, two, it weakens incentives for private investment if firms expect future rescue, and three, it can crowd out spending on higher-return public goods like skills, infrastructure, or energy transition.

Second, a warmer EU relationship may deliver limited economic upside while reopening politically toxic Brexit conflict. One, the UK is outside the single market and customs union, so gains from a youth scheme or summit rhetoric are marginal compared with full market access, two, regulatory concessions may be politically costly without guaranteed growth, and three, the government risks spending scarce political capital on symbolic Europe policy instead of domestic productivity reforms.

Third, the speech itself signals weakness rather than a credible growth plan. One, it is framed as a leadership defence against internal doubters, which undermines confidence in execution, two, broad claims about 'stories' and 'hope' do not substitute for concrete supply-side reform, and three, markets and voters may read this as reactive politics rather than a coherent economic strategy.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether state intervention and EU re-engagement are seen as pragmatic fixes to structural underperformance or as expensive symbolism that distracts from deeper productivity reform. Prop wins if the round is about strategic capability and trade friction; opp wins if the focus is fiscal risk, weak marginal gains, and the danger of politicising economic policy.

THBT the UK should pursue closer economic integration with the EU
THP a world where governments prioritise strategic industrial capacity over market efficiency
THBT Labour should make rejoining European youth mobility schemes a central economic priority

cards.title: Starmer’s Reset Speech Signals a High-Stakes Battle Over Labour’s Economic Credibility
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave a speech aimed at resetting his premiership after Labour’s poor performance in the local elections held the previous week. He said he took responsibility for the result and declared that he knew he had “doubters” and would “prove them wrong.” The remarks come amid pressure on Labour to demonstrate competence, stability, and a credible governing agenda after early electoral setbacks.

prop_args.thesis: Starmer’s willingness to publicly own Labour’s setbacks and reset his premiership strengthens the government by restoring credibility and creating room to govern effectively.
mechanisms: First, public accountability rebuilds trust with swing voters and markets. This is because (1) it signals that the government is responsive rather than defensive, (2) it reduces the perception of chaos or denial after a bad election result, and (3) it gives undecided voters a reason to believe the leadership can learn and adapt.

Second, a reset allows Labour to re-anchor the agenda around competence instead of internal party drama. Three reasons: one, it shifts media attention away from local election losses and toward policy delivery; two, it helps the government discipline its own backbenchers by setting a clear line; three, it improves the odds of passing difficult economic reforms because investors and civil servants value predictability.

Third, proving doubters wrong matters because governing parties are judged on trajectory, not just one electoral setback. This matters because (1) local elections are often low-salience protest votes, (2) early course correction can prevent a temporary dip from becoming a long-term collapse in support, and (3) a more credible leadership image can preserve Labour’s ability to implement unpopular but necessary fiscal choices.

opp_args.thesis: Starmer’s reset is mostly performative and will not solve the deeper political and economic problems driving Labour’s weakness.
mechanisms: First, a speech cannot fix structural voter dissatisfaction. One, local election losses usually reflect real anger over living standards, public services, and trust; two, simply saying 'I will prove them wrong' does not change household finances or policy outcomes; three, if the government lacks a clear economic dividend, rhetoric will be read as empty branding.

Second, the reset may expose weakness rather than strength. One, publicly admitting the need to prove doubters wrong invites more scrutiny and frames the premiership as already on the back foot; two, it can embolden internal critics and opposition parties by signaling vulnerability; three, if the government keeps changing tone, it risks looking directionless rather than decisive.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether political credibility can be rebuilt through leadership signalling or only through material economic improvement. Prop wins if you think early course correction prevents a spiral of distrust; opp wins if you think voters and markets care far more about delivery than messaging.

This House would prioritize political credibility over short-term popularity in economic governance

cards.title: Impeachment of Sara Duterte Becomes a Fight Over Dynastic Succession and Marcos Control of the Philippine State
cards.background: The Philippine House of Representatives voted on Monday to impeach Vice-President Sara Duterte for a second time, sending the case to the Senate for trial. If convicted, Duterte would be disqualified from holding public office and could be blocked from running for president in 2028. The case centers on alleged misuse of public funds and public threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife, and his cousin, House Speaker Martin Romualdez. Duterte was impeached on the same grounds in 2025, but the Supreme Court blocked that attempt on a technicality before trial.

prop_args.thesis: Impeaching Sara Duterte is necessary to enforce accountability and prevent a dynastic, anti-institutional politician from capturing the presidency.
mechanisms: First, it restores the credibility of formal accountability institutions. This is because (1) Duterte is accused of misuse of public funds, (2) she publicly threatened political violence against top state figures, and (3) failing to punish that behavior signals that elite officeholders are above the law.

Second, it blocks a high-risk succession path for a politician who already has mass support and institutional leverage. Three reasons: one, she is leading early presidential surveys by 17 points, two, she has a national platform as vice-president, and three, allowing her to run unchallenged would normalize impunity as a viable electoral strategy.

Third, it reduces the chance that the Philippines becomes trapped in a personalized vendetta politics cycle. This matters because the Marcos-Duterte split has already turned state institutions into weapons in a family feud, and a successful impeachment creates a deterrent against future executives using public office as a shield for patronage and intimidation.

opp_args.thesis: The impeachment is politically motivated elite warfare that weakens democratic legitimacy and risks turning institutions into tools for factional elimination.
mechanisms: First, the process looks like selective prosecution rather than neutral rule enforcement. One, the case was revived after a prior impeachment was blocked on a technicality, two, the House is dominated by Marcos allies who have incentives to sideline a rival, and three, Duterte herself claims the hearings were politically motivated and refused to participate.

Second, removing Duterte may backfire by deepening polarization and strengthening her martyr narrative. One, she already has a 17-point lead in March polling, two, dynastic politics means her base is highly loyal and can interpret impeachment as persecution, and three, that can consolidate anti-Marcos sentiment ahead of 2028 rather than eliminate it.

Third, the move destabilizes elite bargains that keep Philippine politics governable. One, the Marcos-Duterte alliance won by a landslide in 2022 and then collapsed, two, impeachment escalates the conflict from electoral competition into institutional warfare, and three, in a patronage-based system that can encourage retaliatory use of state power whenever coalitions change.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether impeachment is a genuine anti-corruption safeguard or a factional purge dressed up as legality. Prop wins if you prioritize institutional deterrence and the need to stop a likely future president from normalizing impunity; opp wins if you think the process itself is so politicized that it damages democratic legitimacy and creates a martyr with even stronger electoral appeal.

cards.title: Iran War Shock Forces India to Ration Fuel Consumption and Reopen Energy Security Tradeoffs
cards.background: On 11 May 2026, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged Indians to reduce their use of petrol and diesel and to re-adopt conservation habits from the COVID-19 period. The appeal came as the US-Israeli war on Iran drove steep increases in global fuel prices. India is highly exposed to imported energy and therefore faces immediate inflationary pressure when oil prices spike.

prop_args.thesis: External energy shocks prove India must aggressively reduce fuel dependence and accelerate domestic conservation and transition policies.
mechanisms: First, the price shock transmits directly into household and business costs. This is because (1) India imports most of its crude, so global war-driven spikes hit domestic pump prices quickly, (2) higher diesel and petrol costs raise transport, food, and logistics prices across the economy, and (3) the government then has to choose between inflation and fiscal subsidies.

Second, conservation creates immediate macroeconomic resilience. Three reasons: one, lower demand reduces import bills and protects the current account, two, it gives the state more room to manage inflation without massive subsidies, and three, it reduces vulnerability to future geopolitical shocks from the Gulf.

Third, the crisis strengthens the case for structural energy transition. This matters because repeated oil shocks make renewables, public transport, and efficiency upgrades not just climate policy but national security policy; over time, that lowers India’s exposure to coercion and supply disruption.

opp_args.thesis: Fuel conservation is a temporary coping measure that cannot solve India’s deeper energy vulnerability and may impose unnecessary economic pain.
mechanisms: First, demand restraint does not change the underlying supply problem. One, India still needs oil for transport, industry, and agriculture, two, conservation cannot replace the volumes required for a large economy, and three, the state remains exposed to global price swings until it secures alternative supply or substitutes.

Second, austerity-style conservation can slow growth and hurt the poor. One, higher effective energy costs reduce mobility and consumption, two, small firms and informal workers are hit hardest because they cannot hedge fuel costs, and three, the burden falls disproportionately on lower-income households that spend more on transport and essentials.

Third, the better response is diversification, not rationing. One, India can expand strategic reserves and import diversification, two, it can negotiate long-term contracts and invest in refining and renewables, and three, those tools reduce volatility without asking citizens to absorb immediate sacrifices.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term crisis management and long-term structural resilience. Prop wins if the round is about what states should do when geopolitical shocks hit an import-dependent economy; Opp wins if they can show conservation is mostly symbolic and shifts costs onto consumers without fixing supply dependence.
motion_areas: TH, as India, would prioritize fuel conservation over shielding consumers from price increases during external oil shocks
THBT developing nations should treat energy conservation as a national security policy
THP a world where major import-dependent economies are forced to cut fuel demand during geopolitical crises
